REACHABLE BY CONSTRUCTION, not by luck — `src/ws-create.js` creates exactly this state (`_lockedModel: data.modelLock ? (data.lockModel || data.model || null) : null`, whose own comment says the server latches the first main-thread served model instead), `src/server/boot-restore.js` hydrates it from meta, and `src/lib/session-lifecycle.js` carries `modelLock` and `lockModel` as SEPARATE saved-config keys, so a saved config predating `lockModel` resumes locked-with-no-target. The gate is the engine's OWN predicate, asked (never re-spelled) and asked AFTER `noteServedModel` on purpose, so a record served by anything but the reroute target has already retired the stamp and may latch. A refused latch leaves the target where it already was (null) and loses nothing: the repin no-ops either way (`modelsMatch(served, locked)` ⇒ no repin with the substitute latched).

  **(2) THE RUNG ITSELF REFUSES A TARGET THAT *IS* THE STANDING REROUTE.** Not decoration: `src/ws-handler.js`'s `set-model {lock:true}` with no `lockModel` ALSO adopts `session._servedModel` (the UI row it serves says "Lock to this model" about the model on screen), and a session-meta written by any build with an ungated latch carries the substitute for ever. A rung that decides money may not depend on every writer of a field being careful, so `sessionModelFor` skips the lock when `modelsMatch(_lockedModel, _servedViaFallback.to)`. Falling through invents nothing: `servedDefinesModel` refuses that same served model one line below, so the answer is the pick, else the spawn model — the REQUEST — which is byte-for-byte what r2 answered for this shape (measured, both writers), and whatever the ladder returns, `projectionFamilyFor` still sees the standing cross-family reroute and answers null. The `_lockedModel` writer set is now a PRINTED, source-DERIVED census (7 sites, each classified) because that field decides placement.

  **(3) WHAT A STALE REROUTE STAMP ACTUALLY COSTS.** r3's row promised a stale stamp "costs only CONSERVATISM". Measured on the real engine + real pool: a null projection makes EVERY bucket count, and that can also **refuse a move OFF** a member that is hard-dead, because a candidate is disqualified by a cap OUTSIDE this session's family too — a current member 100 % through its 5-hour window kept its conversation while a free member sat beside it, blocked on an Opus cap the session was not using. It never authorises a billed turn (that is the direction that costs money) and it self-heals at the first main-thread record served by anything else, but the ROW has to say so; r2 strands on the identical fixture, so persisting the stamp only makes the state survive a restart instead of being cleared by one.

  **r3-r2 INVARIANTS.** Putting a field on a money ladder makes every WRITER of that field a money path — re-read them all, and census the set rather than trusting the one the incident pointed at. A model the vendor SUBSTITUTED is never a request, wherever it is copied to. Defence in depth is only defence if each layer has its own control: the latch control alone must show the belt still holding (and this branch's does), and only reverting BOTH reproduces the incident. A fix scoped to the QUESTION beats a fix scoped to the file — but when the second writer is a USER action ("Lock to this model" about the model on screen), leave the user's words alone and make the RUNG refuse; then prove the rung covers that writer with a leg, instead of adding a second guard or a twin predicate. A sentence in a schema row is read by the next round as fact: measure what the state can actually do, including the direction that refuses rather than spends.

**AND THE FACT IS PLACED BEFORE ITS READERS (2026-09-13 r4 — the round-3 verifier's HIGH, reproduced on the REAL pipeline `session-stdout.create` → the registry → `claude-stream-json` on a fake pty, plus the real engine + real pool + real credential symlinks, against the shipped r3-r2 commit).**

  **THE SHAPE r3-r2 DID NOT DRIVE.** Its ordering decision — ask `servedDefinesModel` AFTER `noteServedModel`, so a record served by anything else has already retired the stamp and may latch — is right for the reroute announced by a SEPARATE `system/model_refusal_fallback` record that arrives FIRST, which is the only shape §11 built. The incident's own transcript has the other one, and it is the FIRST announcement: the `fallback` CONTENT BLOCK rides the assistant message whose own `message.model` IS the substitute (frozen tail line 219, `04:42:45.234Z`), and the system twin lands **51 s later** (line 225, `04:43:36.398Z`). Both consumers read the served model at the TOP of their assistant branch while the content-block loop that stamps the reroute sits ~90 lines BELOW, so the gate asked a question this record had already answered and nobody had written down: no stamp ⇒ `servedDefinesModel` says yes ⇒ the latch adopts `claude-opus-4-8` and writes it to session-meta, PERMANENTLY.

  **§12's belt holds the placement only while the reroute STANDS.** The stamp retires at the first record served by something else — and that is exactly what exposes the bad lock: with nothing left to refuse, the lock rung answers the substitute for the life of the conversation, `laneByEvidence` asks for the OPUS cap, finds none on the member, and files a Fable rejection against the PLAN week. Measured end to end on the incident's own member (plan 0.65 alive, Fable spent): `[wall] demoted Member W 7d until 2026-09-15T11:59:08Z` with the Fable cap never marked — the incident's §2 harm, reopened through §11's own fix, from ONE record.

  **THE FIX IS THE ORDER.** `rerouteAnnouncedBy(msg)` is the engine's own rule (one implementation, both feeds ask it; main-thread-only INSIDE the function so neither call site can get it wrong), and both consumers stamp through `noteModelFallback` BEFORE `noteServedModel` and before the latch. The later stamps stay put as belts for the shapes this rung cannot see (a `<synthetic>`-model record, a system record with no assistant record at all) and cost nothing — `noteModelFallback` returns early on `prev.to === to` and leaves `at` alone, so restating a standing reroute moves no byte and writes no meta. The verifier's own clause rides along as a BELT (`!announced` on the latch): a record that ANNOUNCES a reroute never latches, whatever any stamp says. Today either alone refuses this record, which is the point — the ORDER is a property of one function's statement order, one refactor away; the BELT is a property of the RECORD.

  **r4 INVARIANTS.** A fact must be placed before its readers, and "its readers" includes the ones inside the same `if` block. **Two records announcing the same event do not arrive in the same order twice** — drive the fixture from the frozen evidence, not from the shape the last round happened to build. A guard that is only correct because of statement order owes a second guard that is correct about the record, and each owes a control that fails ALONE. A permanent write outlives the transient state that justified it: ask what a stored value means after the condition that produced it is gone. And **a twin is enforced by a DERIVED census, not by a comment** — removing the two lines from `session-brain.js` changes nothing observable in the shape the twin leg drives, so only the grep census over every file that CALLS `noteServedModel(` goes red and names it; the census window is MEASURED and PRINTED (110/64 and 278/226 chars against a 1200 bound) and owes both directions plus a positive control.

UI (user-specified 虚线/浅色): popup bars = light diagonal hatch reading→est with dashed right edge + `est N%` stat; taskbar pies + Agents mini-donuts = light arc for the est delta + dashed outer ring; **ROLL DISPLAY RULE: est < reading ⇒ window reset ⇒ dark collapses to 0, whole arc light (est ≥ reading within one window, so est<reading is the clean discriminator — utils.estDisplayPair, shared client-wide)**. Zero API calls anywhere. Tests: scripts/test-usage-estimator.mjs (35) + dbg-est-shot.mjs (screenshot smoke incl. rolled case + pool row) **准确度度量=delta相对误差(2.368.13, owner纠正): 绝对|pred−act|随刷新频率变小——每分钟刷新任何模型都完美; calib行带u0/predDu/actDu/rel(|actΔ|<2pt时rel:null), 引擎指标usage-est-rel-err-pct只在窗口真动过时发; 诚实口径下14天同源≥2pt配对: 5h捕捉~85%/Fable周~78%/7d仅~61%真实移动——系统性低估待查(外部消费份额漂移/学习滞后)。test-usage-estimator(83)自此进CI gate(此前在gate外=silent-stale类)。** **r2 (2026-09-21): `estimateFor`'s cache-built anchor takes the same scoped `asOf` rule as usage-anchors (the newer of the entry's and the file's stamp).** **B-a5c0 (2.369.164 batch 8) TELEMETRY HYGIENE: the engine's 60 s anchor sweep is ONE step per identity group = `sweepAnchorGroup` here (deps injected: anchors, estimator, costBetween, darkHosts, metric) — no reading newer than the last anchor ⇒ no ledger walk, no calibration, no metric; the calib metric `usage-est-rel-err-pct` (`CALIB_METRIC`, `calibMetricRows`) fires only AFTER `maybeRecord` accepted a NEW anchor, once per moved bucket, detail `account=<id> bucket=<key>` (`__vsMetric(name, value, detail)` carries it). `cliRefreshDrift(est, raw, now)` = the auto-cli loop's drift read: a raw bucket whose `resetsAt` is past is NO control for the logged `drift` (null ⇒ the log says "no drift control", never the 100-point old-window-vs-new number); `triggerDrift`/`moved` still count it so the scheduler's inputs — and the vendor-facing spawn cadence — are unchanged.**

### THE NEW-MEMBER WAKE (2026-09-08, usage-pool-engine `onMemberReadingFresh` / `onMemberLoginSuccess` / `autoCliReady` / `lastMemberReadAt`)

  **WHY IT EXISTS.** The pool re-evaluates on TURN ENDS, on STREAMED usage records, and on a 30 s timer for auto pools. A conversation ARMED on exhaustion produces neither of the first two, and the timer only re-ranks the pool — it never re-examines who is waiting. So "a member became usable" reached nothing: the owner added a subscription mid-exhaustion, the pool parked eight fable conversations on it while it had NO reading, auto-resume re-armed them for a reset EIGHT HOURS out, the auto-cli panel read failed (doubling its backoff 5→10 min), the human ⟳ he tried in between wrote the reading and told the pool nothing, and the only thing that ever released them was him typing. Full journal + the honest boundaries: kb-bugfix-invariants, "A MEMBER BECAME USABLE AND NOBODY NOTICED".

  **ONE EDGE, TWO HALVES.** `onMemberReadingFresh(memberId, why, {at})` ① re-decides every pool the member belongs to (`maybePoolAutoSwitchForPool(id, {force:true})` — `force` drops that pool's 10 s event-KICK gate for this one call, because that gate throttles per-RECORD kicks and a member's FIRST reading is not a kick; the 180 s dwell belt is untouched) and ② re-examines every ARMED session on the member or its pools through auto-resume's own `fireNow(id, why, {cause:'member-usable'})`. **The halves answer different shapes** — and which shape belongs to which half was settled by mutation testing, not by reading: with a conversation ARMED, the PRE-FIRE GATE runs `maybePoolAutoSwitch` itself, so half ② silently does half ①'s work as a side effect of the spending machinery. Half ② is the incident's own shape (already parked on the newcomer ⇒ the per-session pass `continue`s and a switch-driven nudge is structurally unreachable); half ① is the shape where NOBODY is armed (nothing fires ⇒ the gate never runs ⇒ only half ① can move a live conversation off a spent member).

  **IT NEVER SPENDS BY ITSELF.** Releases go through `fireNow → attemptFire`: the 2026-09-07 loop breaker (same-identity quarantine, 3/hour cap, backoff) AND the pre-fire gate that re-verdicts and vetoes. No bypass, by construction. `continueNoticeFor` gained a `cause` because `kind:'now'` can no longer stand in for "a pool switch" — the immediate path has a second caller now, and a card explaining a billed turn must name the thing that caused it ("账号 X 已恢复可用" when nothing switched). `cause` defaults to null, so every pre-existing caller is byte-identical. `armedIds()` is a tiny public accessor on auto-resume rather than the engine reaching into `_armed`: "who is waiting" is a question that module should answer, and a caller holding the map could mutate it.

  **REFUSALS ARE NAMED, AND "NO READING" IS ONE.** `no-reading` / `stale-reading` (>10 min) / `foreign-reading` / `member-not-usable` / `wake-floor` / `no-auto-resume`. Never a verdict of 0 %. Rate-floored per member at 20 s so two refreshes landing together are one wake — and **the floor is stamped only when the wake ACTED**, because a declined wake costs one file read and stamping it would let a producer that called a millisecond before its own cache write eat the wake the real one needed.

  **COMPOSITION, NOT A TWIN.** `readingForeignForWake()` asks the window-fingerprint work (inc-mts8a8mr-ulmm, landed 2.369.73) whether the stored snapshot is really this member's. That work ships TWO rules and this asks the SECOND on purpose: ① the LAG SHADOW is about a reading ARRIVING on a session after that session's link moved (it needs a session, a re-point and an age, and the producers applied it before the snapshot reached disk); ② the WINDOW IDENTITY GUARD `decideReadingTarget` is the question a wake actually has. Reached through the same `establishedWindows()` + `windowGroupOf` the write-time guard uses, so there is ONE predicate — and deliberately NOT named "shadowed", because that word already names rule ①. READ-ONLY: `guardReadingTarget` is the WRITE path and it archives; a wake may only decline. A brand-new member has no established window for anything to contradict, so the incident's own case still acts.

  **THE PRODUCERS — all three, because "a third producer cannot forget it" is only true if you wire the third producer that already exists.** (a) `src/server/account-usage-routes.js` hangs the login half on the SAME transition detection the expiry sweep uses (`loginFingerprint`, read off THE ANSWER THE ROUTE ALREADY HOLDS — never a second credential reader), because all three finalize routes are polled every 3 s for up to 5 min; it gets its OWN latch `lastWakeFingerprint`, deliberately not the sweep's, since two of those routes sweep UNCONDITIONALLY for a documented reason and a shared map would make disabling one side effect disable the other. All five login-success exits wake the record the login LANDED in (`'moved'` ⇒ `movedTo`; the auto-merge exit ⇒ the SURVIVOR — waking the throwaway spawns a panel read for a record about to stop existing and leaves the one the pool holds unread). Fire-and-forget: a login must never wait on, or fail because of, a quota read; the promise is parked on `app.locals._lastLoginWake` as an OBSERVABILITY seam (nothing in production reads it) so a regression cannot pass vacuously by looking too early. (b) `src/usage-routes.js` takes the edge on all three LOCAL rungs of `/api/usage/refresh` (session / cli-panel / bare token) through an injected `onMemberReadingFresh`; the `host` branch takes none — a remote machine's pool is not ours to decide for. (c) the auto-cli loop in server.js, on a successful refresh. **The edge is deliberately NOT inside `refreshViaCliPanel`**: the pre-fire SPEND GATE calls that function too, and a gate that releases conversations as a side effect of asking a question is not a gate.

  **`autoCliReady` + `lastMemberReadAt` serve the auto-cli loop.** NOT READY IS NOT FAILED: the loop skipped on the roster's `loggedIn`, which is `parseAuth`'s boolean — TRUE the moment an accessToken *string* exists, whatever its expiry — so a doubly-expired credential file spawned a panel that could not possibly answer and doubled a backoff that never had a chance (the satisfiable gap `src/login-state.js` exists to close). It now asks `memberLoginState`, the credential-FILE reader the pool's slot validation already uses; the FILE reader is the right one and not `accountLoginState` because this rung is `refreshViaCliPanel`, which DELETES `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` from the child's env and points `CLAUDE_SECURESTORAGE_CONFIG_DIR` at the account's own dir, so a long-lived token cannot serve it. And the login-edge read counts as one of the loop's OWN attempts — two schedulers spawning the SAME child through the SAME rung need ONE attempt clock. **Honest boundary, pinned in the suite:** the "no credentials at all" half was ALREADY covered (`parseAuth` answers false with no file, and the journal shows no auto-cli attempt for the newcomer before its login landed), and the incident's 02:18:40 failure happened with `loggedIn` TRUE, so this guard is NOT claimed to be what would have prevented that failure count.

  **`projectionRereadFor(memberId, nowMs)` serves it too (B-f69c ③, 2.369.163).** The families of the LIVE local claude conversations billed on the member right now (a pooled one through `sessionBillingMember`, a direct one through its own account), each projected through the one rule (`projectionFamilyFor` → `projectCacheForFamily` — test-fable-cap-pool-storm §5b's census counts this as the fourth site), crossed against the member's burn (`usageEstimator.burnFor`) at the hot bar when it serves a hot auto pool, else the hard bar → `{inMs, label, line, pctPerMin, band, fam, burnPtPerMin}` or null (no conversation on it, no burn, nothing crosses). The loop hands `inMs` + `burnPtPerMin` to `decideCliRefresh` (account-pool-auto.js "THE PROJECTION"); a pick is spent on the same `refreshViaCliPanel` and its fresh reading takes this wake, so the pool re-decides on the READING. `projectionBurnMemo(now)` is the per-evaluation burn memo the per-session and default passes share.

  **r2 — HALF ② SERVES ONLY THE CONVERSATIONS NOTHING COULD MOVE (three defects, all reproduced first).** Round 1's half ② filtered on POOL MEMBERSHIP and fired, which is right only in the shape it was written for. **(a)** In every shape where the pool structurally CANNOT move a conversation onto the newcomer, the continue was delivered anyway — billed to the member the conversation was already stuck on, with the in-chat card naming THAT member as "recovered", i.e. the r2 invariant ("a card explaining a billed turn must name the thing that caused it") inverted. Three real production states reach it: a MANUAL pool (`auto:false` — `maybePoolAutoSwitchForPool` returns at the top, so half ① is a no-op), a REMOTE conversation (`s.host` — the per-session pass skips it BY DESIGN), and a COLD pool where half ① DID move the link. Measured on the real engine + real pool + real symlinks, armed by the real rejection producer: master's own mechanisms deliver 0 continues, the round-1 wake delivers 1 — onto a member whose cache reads `utilization: 1, status: "limited"` — and writes `账号 Member F 已恢复可用`. **The pre-fire gate cannot catch it**: `quotaVerdictFor` answers a POOLED scope with "any member usable", which is true and beside the point. **(b)** A COLD pool RESTARTS such a conversation through the client (`pool-auto-switched`) precisely because its CLI cannot re-read credentials — and master's ONLY other `fireNow` call site guards that same spend with `if (a.hot)`. Round 1 had no `hot` gate at all. **The fix asks the fact this module already names**: `fireIdentityFor` — "where would a continue land right now", which is auto-resume's own `fireIdentity` dep, so `attemptFire` re-resolves the very same fact — asked TWICE, before half ① runs and after, because "the wake moved it there" and "it was already there" are different worlds and only the second is half ②'s. A session fires only when it lands on `memberId`, landed there BEFORE half ① too, and (if its scope is a pool) that pool is HOT. When half ① DOES move a conversation, that path fires it itself for a hot pool and restarts it through the client for a cold one — half ② adding a second continue there is a double spend, not a rescue. **What the cold rule COSTS, deliberately:** a cold pool's conversation is released by the TIMED path at its armed reset rather than early. That is latency; firing anyway is money, spent on whichever member the CLI still holds — the restart is a CLIENT action, so with no browser connected nothing restarts and the link says one thing while the CLI bills another, and nothing in this process knows whether a client obeyed a broadcast. **(c)** `continueNoticeFor`'s round-1 reorder was NOT byte-identical for existing callers as claimed: hoisting the `/^account usable again/` arm ABOVE `kind:'now'` changed a PRE-EXISTING pair — the engine's own near-arm (`armIfEnabled(…, 'account usable again')` at scheduleWallProbe) followed by a real pool switch firing with `kind:'now'` — from "账号池已切换到 X" to "账号 X 已恢复可用", describing a switch as a recovery. `cause` may only REFINE master's precedence: `moved` still outranks it (if the pre-fire gate re-pointed us, the continue lands on a member the wake never spoke about, so "the pool switched" is the true sentence), and below `cause` master's order is restored verbatim — all eight reachable pre-existing shapes are now byte-compared against `master:src/server/auto-resume.js`. The pair is also pinned in test-auto-resume-loop §3 beside the DRIFT guard that names both engine strings (191), so the round-1 ordering goes red there on its own. **Honest boundary, in the source and in the suite:** deleting the before/after snapshot changes no outcome TODAY — auto-resume refuses the second fire on its own (`session._arFiring` is raised for the whole gate, and a delivered continue deletes the arm), measured. It stays because half ②'s money-safety must not be OWED to another module's private in-flight flag, and §8f drives that interlock so the claim is not decorative. **r2 invariants** = a wake that RELEASES a conversation must prove the continue lands on the member that became usable, not merely that the member is in the same pool — pool membership is not a spend authorization; **a guard master states with a reason at its own spend site is owed at every new spend site** (`if (a.hot)`); the fact to ask is the one the module already NAMES for that question, asked at both instants that matter; **a claim of byte-identity is a measurement**, not a reading of the diff (round 1's commit asserted it and nothing checked it — the pair it broke is written by the engine 900 lines away); and a redundant guard must SAY it is redundant and hand the suite the mechanism that really protects.

  **Gate:** scripts/test-new-member-wake.mjs (96, fast tier) — real engine + real pool + real per-session symlinks + real auto-resume + the real rejection producer + the real route factory; sixteen product-source mutations all go red, and the three that survived the first draft are why §1c and §3 are written the way they are. §8 (r2) drives mkWorld's `auto:false` / `hot:false` / `host` controls — declared since round 1 and never passed by any leg, which is exactly why the three shapes went unmeasured — and its NEGATIVE CONTROLS are PATCHED COPIES of the real engine written beside it (siblings, or their relative requires do not resolve; each replacement's hit count asserted, unlinked on exit, swept by PID liveness at start, and gitignored so a SIGKILL can never leave the tree dirty for the release gate). Each of the three guards goes red on its own when removed, and so does round 1's `continueNoticeFor` ordering.

### spend-authorizer.js / server/spend-guard.js (THE SPEND CEILING — docs/design-account-hardening.md §4.4c, P9, owner decisions D2 / D3 / D6 / D8; 2026-09-08)

  **WHY IT EXISTS.** Producers in this tree can start a BILLED turn with no per-occurrence owner action, and until this change each carried its own local floor: auto-resume's loop breaker (3 immediate fires per session per hour), the Stop nudge's `s._lastStopNudge`, the jobs engine's 30 s per-conversation flood floor. Every one of them paces ONE producer, every one is per SESSION (nine conversations can be parked on one subscription, and the money is spent by the SUBSCRIPTION), and every one is in memory — so a release restart hands them a fresh budget, on an instance that restarts several times a day. Measured on this instance's own transcripts, ALL of them (a `find -mtime -3` sample lies: it selects FILES, and a long-lived conversation's file carries records from months back): **603 Stop-nudge mini-turns across 72 conversations, 2026-07-10 → 2026-09-09, forcing 999 assistant records that read 536,353,861 cached tokens and wrote 513,458** — peaks of 93 in a day, 184 in a rolling 72 h and **21 on ONE conversation inside ONE hour**. Alongside it, auto-resume once fired **130 billed continues into a wall in one night** (kb-bugfix-invariants, "AUTO-RESUME FIRED 130 TIMES INTO A WALL").

  **THE SHAPE.** `src/spend-authorizer.js` is PURE (imports nothing): the closed `SPEND_REASONS` set, `budgetLimits` (the four D6 numbers as settings, where an explicit `0` is a CHOICE and garbage falls back), `pruneBudget` / `spendCounts` (rolling hour + rolling day, never buckets — and `pruneBudget` returns a NEW object so a refused authorization leaves no half-pruned ledger), `authorizeUnattendedSpend`, `noteUnattendedSpend` (which also decides the 80 % notice, once per axis per window), `overageState` / `overageText`, and the two sentences a refusal and a notice say. `src/server/spend-guard.js` is the ORCH half and the only thing that touches disk, telemetry or the inbox. **TWO PHASE, exactly like the loop breaker's `canFire`/`noteFired`:** `authorize()` answers, `note()` charges — an authorization that never became a turn must not consume budget, and a turn that did happen must be charged even if the caller then fails to render its card.

  **THE UNIT IS THE IDENTITY, AND IT IS NOT A NEW DERIVATION.** The guard's `identityOf` is the engine's OWN `fireIdentityFor` (= `wallSlotFor`'s key: the credential slot a turn started right now would bill), which is why the guard is CONSTRUCTED INSIDE `src/server/usage-pool-engine.js` — every input it needs (the identity, the RAW usage cache for overage, the credential-state reader) is already resolved there, and a second construction site would mean a second set of answers, which is the failure §2 of the design catalogues. server.js re-exports it to the three consumers outside the engine (auto-resume, the delivery ladder, the Stop nudge); the inbox is resolved through a lazy `getUserTodos` because it is created later in boot.

  **WHAT IT REFUSES, AND WHY EACH IS FAIL-CLOSED (P8).** An identity it cannot name (a ceiling nobody can be charged against is not a ceiling — structurally rare, since `wallSlotFor` answers `__global__` for a session with no pool, so this means the wiring is broken, which is exactly when spending must stop) · a reason outside the declared set · a credential state that says it cannot serve · **paid overage in use** (D3b) · each of the three caps. Ignorance is NOT a refusal (P6): an unreadable credential state and an absent overage record both pass.

  **PAID OVERAGE (design §1.4 — captured since 2.289.0 and read by NOBODY).** `cache.overage` / `cache.spend` now have exactly one reader, the PURE `overageState`, asked by the authorizer, by the pool's voluntary-target rule (`overageMemberIds`, setting `pool.avoidOverageMembers`, default OFF per D3's "one week of data first") and by BOTH panels (the taskbar usage popup and Manage Agents, through `overageChip` in `src/lib/usage-source.js`). It matters because with overage ON an account's `utilization` stays under 1 while every token is billed pay-per-use — so `accountRemaining()` ranks the account that is spending real money as the one with the MOST headroom. On this instance the record is present on 6 of 7 subscriptions and reads `inUse:false` (`org_level_disabled`), so the gate is dormant here by measurement, not by hope.

  **THE EDF RESERVE FLOOR (D2).** `decidePoolSwitch` gained `reserveFloorPct` (setting `pool.reserveFloorPct`, engine default 15) and `overageIds`: a member below the floor on its **WEEKLY** budget (never the 5 h burst limiter, and never on an unknown reading) stops being a VOLUNTARY switch/placement target, while a HARD-DEAD current member may still escape onto it — the same two-tier rule the login NEAR window earned, and the escape SAYS which bar it landed on (`toReserve` / `toOverage`, never the login-only `toLoginNear`). Both parameters default to inert in the pure module, so every existing caller decides exactly as it did before. `poolBlockedNotice` learned the shape: when a bar is the ONLY thing that emptied the candidate list the sentence says *"every other member is held back by your spending limits"* and points at Settings → Spending, instead of "out of quota", which prescribes waiting for a reset that has nothing to do with it; a quota-emptied list keeps its old sentence verbatim.

  **THE STOP NUDGE (D8).** Its cooldown is PERSISTED in the guard's store, keyed by the session-status key, and the route takes the NEWER of {the in-memory `s._lastStopNudge`, the record} — so a restart no longer resets it. It also gained an EXIT CONDITION: a session that has NEVER reported a board status is being asked for bookkeeping it does not do, so after `agents.stopNudgeMaxUnanswered` (default 3) unanswered nudges it is not asked again, and any status report resets the count. **Honest boundary:** replayed against this instance's real 603-nudge history the D6 defaults refuse 20 (seven slots) to 55 (one slot) of them — this ceiling is a BACKSTOP against bursts and loops, not a routine throttle, and 63 of the 72 conversations that were nudged received exactly one nudge each, so the exit condition saves nothing on that history either (it bounds the pathological case, and its population is an upper bound because `data/session-status.json` keeps only the live sessions' keys).

  **BOTH MONEY GATES NOW FAIL CLOSED (design §1.4).** `beforeAutoResumeFire`'s `catch { return true; }` and the same shape at the wiring site in server.js each turned any failure of the money gate into a green light — and because there were two, fixing one alone would have stayed green. A throw now refuses the continue, says so, and telemeters `spend-gate-error`.

  **NO NEW VENDOR SURFACE (§ban-safety, design §7).** Every input is a file we already hold: the usage cache the passive capture writes, the credential-state reader the pool already asks, and our own ledger. `scripts/test-vendor-whitelist.mjs` is UNCHANGED by this work, and test-spend-paths asserts that.

  **r2 — FIVE DEFECTS THE ADVERSARIAL VERIFIER FOUND, EACH REPRODUCED FIRST (2026-09-09).**

  ① **The engine's own producer was NOT under the ceiling in production, and the leg that said otherwise was vacuous twice over.** `create()` declared `authorizeSpend = null, noteSpend = null` and `server.js` never passed either (the `create({…})` call lists 18 deps; `grep -c authorizeSpend server.js` = 2, both elsewhere), so the guard at the codex reset credit was DEAD CODE. Reproduced by building the engine exactly as server.js does and feeding the real exhaustion payload (`{type:'task_failed', codexErrorInfo:'usage_limit_reached', resetsAt}`) with `codex.limitResetCredit='auto'`: **at a per-identity hourly ceiling of ZERO the credit is still spent.** Two things hid it. The CENSUS reported the engine GATED because `GATED_RE = /authorizeSpend|spendGuard|spend-authorizer/` matched the file that CONSTRUCTS the guard — so "the four wired consumers are all in the GATED set" was a false green about the one file that is also the construction site. And §9(d) sent `{method:'task_failed', params:{error:{message:…}}}`, which matches **no branch at all** (the engine switches on `payload.type`; `src/harnesses/codex-quota.js` requires `payload.codexErrorInfo` matching `EXHAUSTION_RE`), so `!WROTE` was true for a reason unrelated to the ceiling. Fix: the deps are DELETED and `tryResetCredit` asks the module-local `spendGuard` directly (it is in scope from the construction 1200 lines above and the reset-credit path runs long after the factory returns); `GATED_RE` now matches a CALL (`authorizeSpend(` / `spendGuard.authorize(` / `authorizeUnattendedSpend(`), so a construction line alone no longer satisfies it; the leg drives the production shape with a POSITIVE CONTROL (budget 100/h ⇒ the credit IS spent, proving the path is reached) and asserts the LEDGER in both directions. **Invariant: a gate whose call site depends on a dep the one real caller does not hand over is a gate nobody has — and a census that reads "this file mentions the guard" cannot see a producer inside the file that builds it.**

  ② **An oat-only subscription was refused every unattended turn, for ever, with a false reason.** `credentialStateOf` was wired to `memberLoginState`, the SLOT reader — deliberately oat-blind, because re-pointing a symlink can never hand a long-lived token to a running CLI. Asked about an ACCOUNT it is wrong for B-211a `oatOnly`, a supported and spawnable configuration with **no credential file at all** (`resolveForSpawn` → `{oatOnly:true, localEnv:{CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN}}`). Reproduced against the real AccountManager + the real guard: `loginState(file)` = `{state:'missing', usable:false}` ⇒ auto-resume, the Stop nudge, job notifications, peer messages and the reset credit all `identity-cannot-serve`, and unlike the hour/day caps that refusal never expires — an armed session on such an account waits for ever after a usage limit while the guard files a "For you" item asserting the account is signed out. Fix: a new `accountCredentialState(key)` in the engine asks `accountLoginState(subCredsPath, {oatMintedAt})` (src/login-state.js, the ACCOUNT reader the panels and the repair migration already use) and the guard is constructed with THAT; `memberLoginState` keeps its slot-validation callers untouched. **Invariant: the credential FILE is not the ACCOUNT — a reader written for "does this SLOT hold credentials" answers the wrong question about "can this IDENTITY serve a request right now", and the wrong answer here is permanent.**

  ③ **Every budget above 800 was unenforceable.** `MAX_STAMPS = 4 * 200` truncated both stamp lists while the schema offered `perIdentityDay` up to 2000 and `perInstanceDay` up to 10000 and `budgetLimits` clamped at 100000/1000000. Executed against the shipped module: limits 1000/1000/1000, **1500 charged spends, counts `{hour:800, day:800, instanceDay:800}`, the 1501st AUTHORIZED**. Fix in two halves, because either alone leaves the same class open: retention is now a FUNCTION of the live limits (`stampCap`, still bounded — `CAP_MAX.perInstanceDay + 64`), and `budgetLimits` clamps at `CAP_MAX`, which IS the schema's own `max` row for row. test-spend-paths §1 re-derives those three numbers FROM `src/lib/settings-schema.js`, so widening one row without the other goes red. **Invariant: the offered range and the enforceable range are ONE SET — a setting the UI accepts and the ledger cannot count is a money bound that is not one.**

  ④ **A delivery that opens no turn is not a spend.** `spent()` fired on every accepted delivery, including a `notification` STEERED into a turn already running — which the wrapper folds into that turn (it carries only itself; the queue is untouched) and which bills nothing. Reproduced through the real ladder + the real guard: three mid-turn Background Work notifications charge three turns, and the auto-resume continue on that slot is then refused `hour-cap`; the ceiling is spent on nothing and the thing it exists to bound goes unfunded. **The verifier's suggested fix (charge only when the target is idle) is wrong** and is recorded as such: claude's cli-inbox QUEUES a mid-turn delivery and then runs it as its own billed turn, and a codex `peer` frame is `thread/queue/add`, likewise its own turn afterwards — both are DEFERRED, not free. The free case is exactly one lane: `notificationDelivery(capsOf(backend)) === 'steer'` + `kind === 'notification'` + a turn in flight — a fact read off the caps row, never a backend id. Because that is a PREDICTION (the turn can end between the check and the RPC; a review/compact turn is not steerable), the charge is WITHHELD rather than waived: `settleRpcDelivery(cid, {ok, mode})` settles it from the wrapper's own `peer_message_result` — `mode:'steered'` drops it, `'queued'`/`'turn'` charges it then, `ok:false` charges nothing (the caller re-stashes). The consumer that already reads that record (`src/server/stdout/codex-events.js`) makes the call, by property access on the lazy ref. **Round 2 — a MODE-LESS answer is not an answer about our frame, and the queue holds EVERY frame.** Reproduced: the wrapper has six `peer_message_result` emitters and TWO of the three `ok:false` ones are about a DIFFERENT, earlier message (a queued peer item dropped by Stop, or removed from the queue, handed back so the ladder can re-stash). Round 1 consumed an entry on any answer, so a Stop landing between our write and the wrapper's reply shifted the pending entry and the REAL answer — `mode:'queued'`, a billed `thread/queue/add` — then found an empty queue and charged nothing. The split is exact and is now an ASSERT over the wrapper's own emitters: every `ok:true` carries a `mode`, every `ok:false` carries `text` and no mode. So a mode-less result settles nothing (`'not-ours'`), and the third one (the wrapper's own delivery failure) simply strands its frame, which is charged nothing. Second half: `noteFrameWritten` tracks EVERY rpc-rung frame, charged or not (`withheld` = the charge not made). The wrapper answers in write order, so a queue holding only the predicted-free frames would hand a charged peer message's answer to the notification's entry — and then the notification's own answer would find an empty queue. Third: a frame older than `SETTLE_TTL_MS` (120 s, >4× the wrapper's own 30 s `thread/queue/add` budget) is STRANDED and dropped rather than left to absorb the next message's answer. **Invariants: over-charging a money ceiling is not the conservative direction — it spends the bound that protects the expensive events on events that cost nothing; a correlation-free settlement must derive its match rule from the PRODUCER's own emitters (and assert that derivation), and it must track every frame it wrote or the ordering it relies on is not the ordering it has.**

  ⑤ **The paid-overage refusal had no staleness bound.** `overageState` captured `asOf` and nothing consumed it, so `inUse:'yes'` refused every unattended turn indefinitely and `retryAfter` printed a reset instant in the PAST; the record only self-heals on a NEW `rate_limit_event` carrying a defined overage field, and an auto-resume-armed session is by definition idle and produces none. Measured on this instance's seven live records: `asOf` ages 0 h, 2 h, 5 h, 5 h, 5 h, 21 h and **33 h — the 33 h one on a cache file refreshed 4 minutes ago** — and **0 of 7 carry a `resetsAt` at all**, which is why a window of hours would flip live accounts to 'unknown' (and 'unknown' ALLOWS) while `resetsAt` alone would be inert here. Fix: the blocking claim expires two ways — its own `resetsAt` in the past (a period that ENDED is not a statement about now, which also removes the past `retryAfter`) or `asOf` older than `OVERAGE_STALE_MS` (7 days, >5× the longest gap measured here) — and an UNDATED record cannot claim the present either. The record keeps `stated` and names the rung in `evidence`, so a refusal is never mistaken for a stale file; `inUse:'no'` is deliberately NOT bounded (it blocks nothing). The refusal detail now carries the age. Because the panel chip is gated on the same `inUse === 'yes'`, its tip ("Automatic turns are refused on this account") and the gate can no longer disagree. Dormant here by measurement: all seven records read `inUse:false`. **Invariant: only the claim that BLOCKS needs a date, and it needs one — ignorance is never a claim, and neither is a month-old assertion about the present.**

  **r3 — THREE MORE, EACH REPRODUCED FIRST (2026-09-09).**

  ① **The `Spending` settings category was never rendered, so every ceiling this work added was unreachable in the product.** `SETTINGS_CATEGORIES` (`src/lib/settings-schema.js`) is not an ordering hint — it IS `SettingsUI._renderContent`'s render loop: the method groups every row by `schema.category`, creating a bucket for whatever it finds, and then renders by iterating THAT ARRAY, so a category nobody listed is grouped and dropped. Replaying that loop verbatim over the real schema: **118 settings, 108 rendered, 10 NEVER RENDERED** — the seven `spend.*` / `pool.*` rows this work added (every money ceiling, the overage consent, the EDF reserve floor) plus three `opencode.*` rows that had been invisible since the day they shipped. Replaying it with a search query: `unattended` → 5 rows match, **0 sections rendered** ⇒ the panel prints "No settings match your search."; `overage` → 2 match, 0 rendered. There is no second write path — `serverSetting()` reads the sparse `data/settings.json` and only this UI writes it (measured on the live instance: 30 keys, none `spend.*`). Consequences that were live: `pool.reserveFloorPct` defaulted to 15 and changed every pool switch/placement decision with no way to set it back to 0; the guard's own "For you" item, the pool's blocked notice and the overage chip all told the user to open **Settings → Spending**, a place that could not be opened; `docs/settings.md` documented a section the UI could not show. Nothing was red because no suite compared the two sets — which is exactly why the second omission (OpenCode) could ride in behind the first. Fix: two array entries, plus **`test-architecture.mjs` §44**, a build-time census that asserts the CONSEQUENCE (`every setting reaches a rendered section`, 118/118) as well as set inclusion, pins the UI's own coupling (`for (const cat of SETTINGS_CATEGORIES)` still being the render loop), fails an EMPTY listed category too (the dead-allowlist rule in the other direction), and carries both controls — a synthetic row in an unlisted category must be dropped, and listing that category must be the whole fix. **Invariant: an ordered list that a renderer ITERATES is a switch, not documentation — every producer of a category owes it an entry, and the census belongs in the build because the defect is one missing array element in a file every feature touches.**

  ② **The pre-fire money gate still failed OPEN at auto-resume's own layer.** Design P8 is "money gates fail CLOSED, at EVERY layer"; §1.4 named two (the engine's `catch { return true; }` and the `server.js` wiring lambda) and r2 fixed those two — but `src/server/auto-resume.js` has a THIRD, its own: `try { gate = beforeFire(id, session); } catch { gate = true; }` and `.catch(() => deliver())`. r2 verified the fix by GREPPING the two other files, so nothing ever drove this one. Reproduced against the REAL module with the shape of the suite's own §9 harness: `beforeFire` returns false ⇒ 0 continues (control), returns true ⇒ 1 (control, the gate is reached), **THROWS ⇒ 1 billed continue delivered, returns a REJECTED PROMISE ⇒ 1**. It is masked in production (the engine's body is wholly inside its own try/catch so the promise cannot reject, and the wiring lambda catches synchronous throws), but the mask lives in two different files from the bug, and making that lambda `async` — the natural refactor, since the callee already is — removes both halves of it at once. Fix: one named `gateFailedClosed(id, how, e)` (journal line naming the layer + `spend-gate-error` telemetry, matching the engine's), `gate = false` on a throw, and the rejection handler NEVER calls `deliver()`; the arm is untouched, exactly as for a `false` verdict — the promise still stands, it is the gate that is unavailable, and the next tick asks again. The rejection handler is the SECOND argument of `then`, not a trailing `.catch`: master's `.catch(() => deliver())` also caught a throw from `deliver()` itself (`save()` on a full disk, a throwing emit handler) and answered it by calling `deliver()` **a second time** — so the delivery's own failure now gets its own journal line and no retry, and the "the gate rejected" sentence stays an assertion that is true. §9 DRIVES all four arms and keeps a **patched copy of the real module** with master's two shapes restored as the negative control (both substitutions asserted to have landed, and both asserted byte-identical to `40ad936d:src/server/auto-resume.js` so the control reproduces the SHIPPED defect rather than an invented one; it delivers 1 continue on each). **Invariant: a defence-in-depth rule means the layer must be verified AT that layer — a source regex read on two other files proves nothing about the third, and a mask that lives in a different file from the bug is one refactor from gone.**

  ③ **The producer census was FILE-granular, so a new producer added to any already-gated file was invisible.** `censusOver` computed one verdict per FILE and every primitive match inherited it — the same class as ①'s r2 defect, one level up, and those four files are exactly where the next producer is most likely to land. Reproduced by replaying the shipped body over a scratch file holding BOTH a correctly gated Stop-nudge arbiter AND a new ungated `formatChatInput` producer: verdict `GATED`, unwired count **0**. Fix: the verdict is per SITE, and "gated" means a gate call is still IN SCOPE ABOVE it — you ask before you spend, and the asking has to be in the same function. Scope is decided by INDENTATION rather than a byte window, because a window big enough for the real code (measured: the delivery ladder's own gate sits **6,285 chars** above its last rung) is bigger than most files and would call the scratch file above gated too — the control would be theatre. Three properties the measurements forced: whole-line comments are BLANKED first (auto-resume's JSDoc reads `@param deps.authorizeSpend (id, session, identity) => …`, which satisfies a call-shaped regex — r2's "a CALL, never a mention" rule was true of the regex and false of the input it ran on); an anchor may be a call to a LOCALLY GATED HELPER (auto-resume asks through `spendOk(…)` on the line directly above its send, and a census that reddens on correct code is one somebody deletes); and a one-line `const x = (() => {…})()` is not an enclosure (deriving the enclosing function from "the nearest header line above" picked exactly such a sibling in `agent-routes.js` and mislaid the real Stop-nudge gate). `ALLOW` is keyed by **(file, primitive)** — a whole-file pass would re-open the hole this round closed — and two rows the per-site verdict made explicit joined it: agent-routes' forward to the gated ladder, and the ladder's own header. The census now prints 20 SITES with the anchor that gated each. Controls: the mixed file (the new producer UNWIRED while the gated one stays GATED, with the retired file-granular verdict shown calling that whole file gated), a JSDoc-only "gate" (unwired, and shown gated without comment-stripping), and a live scope pin that the real tree contains ≥2 files holding both kinds of site. Mutation-tested on the product source: appending an ungated producer to `src/server/conversation-deliver.js` reports `:340 [user-frame] UNWIRED` and turns the census red; removing the ladder's gate call turns four sites red. **Invariant: a census answers per SITE or it answers about the file that happens to contain the site — and its scope rule has to be measured against the real code before the control it enables is worth anything.**


  **r4 — TWO MORE, EACH REPRODUCED FIRST (2026-09-09); plus one this branch found by mutation-testing its OWN new leg.**

  ① **The ladder AUTHORIZED against one credential slot and DEBITED a different one, so the per-identity ceiling could be bypassed indefinitely on the authorized account while an account nobody asked started refusing its own legitimate unattended turns.** `deliverToConversation` resolves `identity` as `session ? null : {…}` — deliberately null on the local-session branch, because a live local session answers the question by itself — and then handed that null straight to the charge: `charged = { reason, session, identity }`. `spend-guard.note()` therefore ran `identityFor(session, undefined)` → `identityOf(session)` → the engine's `fireIdentityFor` **a second time, at charge time**, which is the one question this whole design exists to have exactly one answer to. The gap is not theoretical and the rpc rung makes it wide ON PURPOSE: that rung WITHHOLDS the charge and defers it to `settleRpcDelivery`, up to `SETTLE_TTL_MS` = 120 s later, while a codex session's slot follows the pool DEFAULT (the engine's per-session pass skips codex outright, `usage-pool-engine.js` `if ((s2.backend || 'claude') === 'codex') continue;`) and `maybePoolAutoSwitchForPool` re-decides that default on its own 30 s timer. REPRODUCED against the real guard + the real ladder (real codex rpc session, real wrapper sidecar caps, `spend.unattendedPerIdentityHour = 1`, `identityOf` flipping A→B between the frame write and the wrapper's `peer_message_result{mode:'queued'}`): **three deliveries all authorized `ok:true` against a cap of ONE**, the ledger reading `{B: 3}` and `{A: 0}` — A's ceiling never bound because A was never debited, and B, which was never asked, now refuses its own auto-resume continue. The damage runs both ways, which is why one ledger assertion is not enough. The other three producers escaped it for reasons that are properties of how their code is currently arranged, not of the question being asked once: auto-resume hands the identity it re-checked after the pre-fire gate (`ident2`), and the Stop nudge and the codex reset credit re-resolve with no `await` in between. **The PURE verdict already carried the answer** (`authorizeUnattendedSpend` returns `identity` on both the ok and the refusal path) — throwing it away was the whole defect. Fix: `charged = { reason: spendReason, session, identity: (v && v.identity) || identity }`, and the same rule stated at the other three pairs (`spendOk` hands its verdict's slot back through an out-param, the Stop route declares `auth` outside the gate block, the reset credit keeps `av` in scope) — because "nothing awaits in between" is a property of an arrangement of code, not of the question having one answer. **The guard now says when the rule is broken in PRODUCTION**: a `note()` that arrives with a session and no identity still charges (a dropped charge is the money-unsafe direction) but increments `chargesUnhinted`, journals once per 5 min and emits `spend-charge-unhinted` telemetry; the suite drives all four producers and asserts that counter is 0, which is the census a grep over five call sites cannot be, plus a control that a charge carrying only a session really does move it.

  ② **The design's §1.4 row was marked CLOSED while one of the three fields it names still had zero readers.** The row names `cache.overage`, claude's `spend {used,limit,pct}` and codex's `spendControlReached`; r3's verdict read "one reader (`overageState`, PURE)", and `overageState` reads the first two only — `grep -rn spendControlReached src/` returned exactly two hits, both in its WRITER (`src/harnesses/codex-quota.js`). Not a money leak (codex REJECTS a spend-controlled account's requests rather than billing them) but the leak the row itself describes is real for it: nothing marks a window spent, so `accountRemaining()` reads a friendly `utilization` and both panels draw friendly donuts for an account that cannot serve a single request — and it ranks as the member with the most headroom. **The record was the defect**, because that row is what the next round reads to decide what is left to build, so the fix is both halves. The field gets the SAME one reader: PURE `spendControlState` beside `overageState`, three-state, dated on the SAME `OVERAGE_STALE_MS` constant (imported, not re-declared — a second window for one physical fact is how twins are born), with only the claim that BLOCKS bounded (`reached:'no'` is deliberately not date-bounded). It refuses under its own name `spend-control-reached` in the `identity-cannot-serve` class, NOT the money one — `spend.allowOverageTurns` deliberately does not unlock it, because that setting consents to SPENDING money, not to being refused by the vendor. Both panels render `spendControlChip` from the same verdict, so a chip can never disagree with the gate. **Honest boundary, measured on this instance:** one codex snapshot in `data/usage-cache` carries the field today and its value is `null` — no claim, so nothing is blocked and no chip is drawn (exactly P6). This wiring is therefore a BACKSTOP whose live effect is currently zero; what was fixed is that the field now has a reader at all, and that the record no longer says otherwise. And the ROW becomes ENFORCEABLE: §7b walks the fields the row claims, fails on any with no PURE reader in the authorizer, requires the row's own verdict to NAME the reader of every field it claims, and keeps r3's verdict text beside it as the control that this check can go red.

  ③ **Found by mutation-testing r4's own new leg: an assert that could not fail.** §5c's "a peer message charged on delivery is charged to the authorized slot too (the await is the window)" put the awaiting `postToPeer` behind a `findPeer` that answered `null`, so the transport was never called and the ladder ran from the gate to the rpc rung's charge SYNCHRONOUSLY — the driver's re-point landed after the money had already moved. MEASURED both ways: an order probe on the real ladder printed `authorize → CHARGE → (the driver re-points)` with `postToPeer` never called, and the leg stayed GREEN with the product fix reverted while the four legs around it went red. The rung is now reached (`livePeer`), a CONTROL asserts the delivery really rode it before the money is read, and under the same mutation the leg now goes red. **Invariant: a fixture that names the mechanism it relies on ("the await is the window") has to REACH it — and the way you find out is to mutation-test your own new legs, not only the product code they were written for.**

  **r4 invariants.** **CHARGE WHAT YOU AUTHORIZED**: the authorizer is entitled to resolve the slot and its verdict CARRIES it precisely so the charge can name the same one; a charge that re-derives the identity asks a mutable question twice, against state our own handlers are free to have moved in between, and the two-phase split (authorize answers, note charges) makes that window as wide as the settlement. **A rule that holds "because nothing awaits in between" is a property of an arrangement of code, not of a design** — state it at every pair, and give it a production counter rather than a grep. **A record that says a thing is finished must name every field it claims** — the row is what the next round reads, so a verdict covering two of three named fields is a defect in the one artefact that decides what gets built. **Only the claim that BLOCKS needs a date**, and a second staleness window for one physical fact is a twin. **An assert that cannot fail is not an assert** — including the ones this round wrote.
  **r5 — TWO MORE, EACH REPRODUCED FIRST (2026-09-09).**

  ⑬ **The ledger was pruned at BOOT with the DEFAULT limits, so every restart forgave spend an owner-raised cap had counted.** r2's ③ made retention a function of the caps — but the one place it is applied to the ledger ON DISK cannot know them: the guard is built inside `usage-pool-engine.create()` (`server.js:434`) and `serverSetting` reads `persistenceRouter.readSettings`, which `setupPersistence()` assigns **318 lines later** (`server.js:752` → `src/routes/persistence.js:600`). Measured at that instant against the real router: `readSettings = undefined`, `budgetLimits() = {12,60,200,80}` (the DEFAULTS), `stampCap = 264`. Reproduced on the real guard: 500 same-day stamps + an owner day cap of 500 came back holding 264, so the guard authorized **236 more unattended turns today instead of 0** — on every boot, and pruning only DROPS, so the later `note()` calls (which do use live limits) can never put them back. Fix: `A.LOAD_RETENTION` (`CAP_MAX` + headroom = 10064 stamps — the widest any offerable cap can count) is what the loader prunes with, and the first `note()` re-prunes with the live limits. The two error directions are not symmetric: over-retention is bounded memory, under-retention is money. **Invariant: a module constructed before its settings reader exists must not make an IRREVERSIBLE decision with limits nobody can answer yet.**

  ⑭ **Authorize and charge are not one instant, so the ceiling was bypassed by the in-flight concurrency count.** The ladder authorizes SYNCHRONOUSLY and charges after an awaited transport (up to 120 s later on the rpc rung), with nothing in between re-reading the ledger and nothing reserving — so N deliveries dispatched in one pass all read the same pre-charge counts. Reachable in production: `src/jobs.js` fires `deliverToConversation` fire-and-forget from loops over `this.jobs.values()` (run-completion and the boot catch-up pass) and `/api/agent/msg/send` is a concurrent HTTP route into the same ladder, while the 30 s `_notifyRate` floor is keyed PER CONVERSATION and does not serialise across them. Measured with the real guard + real ladder, cap 2/hour, five conversations on ONE slot: **5 delivered, 5 charged**; sequentially: 2. `chargesUnhinted` stays 0, so r4's counter cannot see this shape. Fix in the AUTHORIZER, not the ladder (the other three producers run authorize → act → note with no await): `authorize()` returns `v.hold`, an in-memory reservation `pendingCounts` adds to the caps exactly like a charge until `note()` converts it, `release()` gives it back, or it expires at `RESERVE_TTL_MS` = 3 min — **> the ladder's own 120 s settle window** (a frame waits that long for the wrapper's verdict) and **≪ the hour** it is counted in, which is what lets `pendingCounts` answer one number per scope rather than a second windowed accounting. A hold is NOT a stamp: the stash rung opens no turn, so it gives the hold back — at **ONE** release point (a `finally` in `deliverToConversation`, because the ladder has nine exits plus two throwing catches and enumerating them is the fragility). A withheld rpc frame is released when the wrapper CONFIRMS the steer, charged when it says the frame became a turn, and released when a later answer sweeps it as STRANDED. Holds are not persisted on purpose — a restart kills the in-flight deliveries they stand for. **Two shapes the fix forced, both pinned:** a PROBE must not hold (`authorize({hold:false})` — auto-resume asks the ceiling BEFORE its pre-fire gate and again after it, and with the first call reserving the second refused its own request: measured at cap 1/hour, zero continues ever fired), and **the rungs must stay in the same function as the gate** (round 1 split them into a helper and §2's per-site census went red on all four rungs — correctly, because a helper the gate merely calls is exactly the shape that census exists to catch). The guard publishes `holdsOpen`/`holdsExpired` for the same reason r4 published `chargesUnhinted`: a hold nobody converted or released is a producer that authorized a spend and never said what happened, and that is not something a grep can see.

  **GATE: scripts/test-spend-paths.mjs (308, fast tier) + test-architecture §44 (in `npm run build`).** §2 is the grep-derived CENSUS — the file set is `git ls-files -- src server.js data/bin` minus `src/lib/` (the browser cannot spend), the primitives are the six ways to put a turn into a live session, the walked set is PRINTED, non-spending files are an allowlist WITH a reason where a row that stops matching FAILS, a synthetic producer in a scratch tree is the negative control and the same producer wired to the authorizer is the positive one; both directions of the reason table are asserted (an undeclared reason would be refused at runtime; a declared-but-unused one is a slot the next producer slides into without a decision). The rest drives the REAL modules: the real engine + real pool + real symlinks + real auto-resume for the ceiling and the arm that survives it, the real delivery ladder for "a refusal STASHES and nothing is lost", the real Stop-check route for the persisted cooldown and the exit condition, and four fail-closed sites. **r2 added:** §1's schema⇄clamp census (with an "the census can read the schema" assert so it cannot pass vacuously) and the overage-evidence rungs; §2's permanent control for r2's own blind spot (a file that CONSTRUCTS the guard but never ASKS it must read UNGATED, with the retired regex kept beside it as the proof that it would not have); §3b's oat-only account through the REAL engine's two readers, with a wiped-and-no-token account as the negative control; §5b's steer legs with THREE positive controls (idle codex ⇒ charged, human peer mid-turn ⇒ charged, claude mid-turn ⇒ charged) so the exception can never widen silently; and §9(d) rebuilt on the real payload with its own positive control. **Round 2 added** the wrapper-emitter census (with an "all six were found" assert so it cannot pass vacuously), the Stop-drop interleaving leg, the ordering leg (a charged peer frame written first must not take the notification's settlement) and the stranded-frame leg with its in-window control. Each of the five fixes was mutation-tested against the product source: reverting it turns 1–6 asserts red and restoring it returns ALL PASS. **r3 turned §2 into a PER-SITE census** (comment-blanked source, gated-helper anchors, indentation scope, an ALLOW keyed by (file, primitive), the printed set now naming every site and the anchor that gated it, plus the mixed-file and JSDoc-only controls and the retired file-granular verdict kept beside both) and **§9 into a DRIVEN leg for auto-resume's own pre-fire gate** (throw / rejected promise / both controls, with a patched copy of the real module as the negative control) while keeping the two source pins for the layers that are read rather than driven — and it added `test-architecture` §44, the settings-category census, because the seven settings this suite guards were unreachable in the UI. **r4 added** §5c — the charge-names-the-authorized-slot leg, driven on all four producers through their REAL modules, with a patched copy of the real ladder carrying r3's shipped line as the negative control (byte-compared against `4ceba626` so the control reproduces what shipped rather than an invention), a control that the identity really moves between two questions, and a control that the guard's `chargesUnhinted` counter is reachable at all — and §7b, which walks the fields the design's §1.4 row CLAIMS and fails on any without a PURE reader, with r3's own verdict text as the control that it can go red. **r5 added** §1's reservation rules (including the TTL as a RELATION to the ladder's settle window, not a taste), §3d (the production boot ordering pinned on the real files, then the real ledger driven through it, plus a bound on what the wide retention can cost), §5d (five concurrent deliveries on one slot, with the sequential run on an identical world as the positive control and the stash rung's release measured on the SAME identity — the ladder charges a conversation it cannot see locally to a named `__unattributed__` bucket, so a leg that used one would have proved nothing) and §5e (the probe, the withheld steer with all three wrapper answers, and the hold census with a control that it is reachable). Every negative control here is a PATCHED COPY of the real module through one shared `mutantModule` helper, and all six mutations — boot prune, no hold, no release, a probe that holds, no give-back at settle, no give-back when stranded — were verified red before restoring. **B-59b8 (2.369.164 batch 5) added §4b** — the release on auto-resume `deliver()`'s two NON-DELIVERING exits, which the merge verifier had measured unpinned (deleting either `giveBack()` left this suite, test-auto-resume and test-auto-resume-loop green): at an hour cap of ONE, a refused send (`sendToSession` → false, "will retry") and a verb gone at fire time (`resumeVerb` stubbed: present at arm, null at fire) each leave `holdsOpen === 0` and the SAME slot authorizes the next continue (the failed send keeps its arm and its retry lands, charged once; the no-verb exit disarms by design and a second arm lands); `mkWorld` gained `send` / `resumeVerb` / `arModule` for it. Each exit has its own patched-copy negative control (that exit's `giveBack();` removed ⇒ its leg red with the hold still booked, the OTHER leg still green), and both were also verified red by editing the real file before restoring.

### login-state.js / slot-transitions.js / reading-repair.js / reading-lag.js (READINGS BY SLOT, 2026-09-07; + the LAG SHADOW and the WINDOW IDENTITY GUARD, 2026-09-08)
  **THE ROOT CAUSE (owner: "为啥不是从根源上解决假数据而是加 guardrail").** Every VALUE reading — statusline ingest, `rate_limit_event` capture, limit-banner marks, the auto-cli panel result, the anchors they feed, and the OTel "corrections" — was keyed by `orgVerifiedKey()` = the OTel-observed org. That org is the identity the CLI cached in its config dir at SPAWN, while the credentials a RUNNING CLI reads can be re-pointed later (2.1.257 `rpe()` re-reads `.credentials.json` on an mtime change — exactly what the pool's hot switch does). So after any hot switch a session's readings were filed under the account it was SPAWNED on, forever. Two faces: the VISIBLE one (this instance's Member P, credentials emptied 2026-09-03T05:55Z, still receiving limit-banners on 09-07 — measured, see below) and the SILENT one (between two logged-in members a Fish-billed session spawned under Member B files Fish's numbers under Member B; nothing looks wrong at all). 2.369.66 had already fixed the BLOCKING half the same way (`rejectionSlotFor`/`wallSlotFor`/`sessionBillingMember`); this is the VALUE half. A "logged-out members reject readings" guardrail was explicitly REJECTED as the fix — logged-out members are the symptom.
  **THE ONE RESOLVER.** `readingSlotFor(session, at)` (usage-pool-engine) = the validated credential slot, PINNED FOR THE TURN and cleared by `noteTurnEnd` — the exact twin of `rejectionSlotFor`, deliberately sharing `wallSlotFor`'s body, because a reading and a rejection are facts about the SAME thing. The pin exists for the same reason: every producer calls `maybePoolAutoSwitch` the moment it writes, so one turn's ~20 readings would otherwise be split across the members our own re-points moved to while they were arriving. A re-point reaches the CLI on its NEXT request, so the turn boundary is when a switch becomes true. `resolveUsageKey` now resolves `sessionBillingMember` too, and **`sessionReadingMember` and `orgVerifiedKey` are DELETED** — keeping two functions for one question was the bug's home, and the one that was wrong owned every value on the instance. The observation survives as `corroborateReading()`: it logs the divergence once per session per 10min, telemeters `usage-reading-observation-diverged`, and stamps `corroborated:true|false` on the cache write as a LABEL. `resolveUsageKey`'s fallback also learned the backend (`__global_codex__` vs `__global__`) — one resolver serving both CLIs has to know they are different identities.
  **THE STATUSLINE half.** `data/bin/vibespace-usage` was keyed by `VIBESPACE_ACCOUNT_KEY`, fixed at SPAWN, with a comment claiming "a hot re-point is a known attribution seam handled by the ledger's time-based records" — wrong on both halves (the CLI does re-read, and the statusline cache is not the ledger). ws-create now also ships `VIBESPACE_ACCOUNT_LINK` = the credential SYMLINK the CLI reads (`spawnAccount.localEnv[CLAUDE_SECURESTORAGE_CONFIG_DIR]`, i.e. the per-session plan-C link or the pool default) and the tool `readlink`s it per write — the slot resolved by the process that produced the reading. The REMOTE branch deliberately has no twin: a host gets its credentials tarred at spawn and the engine's re-points skip host sessions, so there is no later switch to be wrong about.

  **THE LAG SHADOW + THE WINDOW IDENTITY GUARD (inc-mts8a8mr-ulmm, 2026-09-08; `src/reading-lag.js`).** The slot rule above is right and stays. What it could not know is that the link moves while requests are IN FLIGHT. Owner report: *"a low-usage account suddenly jumped to 93% 7d"*. Timeline, from this instance's own stores: `05:27:00Z` the pool moved 9 sessions Member Y→Member P (`slot-transitions.jsonl`, 9 per-session rows + 1 default row) · `05:27:16Z` a response to a request made 39 s earlier WITH MEMBERY'S TOKEN arrived; `readingSlotFor` had resolved the turn's slot at its first reading = Personal, so Member Y's 93 % 7d was filed on Personal — the anchor is still on disk, Member P's own anchor stream at 05:27:39 with `sevenDay {u:0.93, resetsAt:1789030800}` beside a `fiveHour` and a `scopedWeekly` that are Personal's own (a `rate_limit_event` names ONE bucket, so a lag-shadowed reading poisons exactly that one and leaves the rest correct — which is why the record is self-identifying) · `05:28:38Z` the pool read Personal as "5 % left" and moved everything to Member F · `05:29:39Z` Personal's own `/usage` panel restored it to 13 % · `05:31:40Z` the pool moved everything back. **Two false switches in 98 seconds, caused by our own write.**

  **THE EVIDENCE THE RESPONSE CARRIES ABOUT ITSELF.** A rate-limit payload names the WINDOW its numbers are counted in, and a weekly window is an ACCOUNT FINGERPRINT. Measured over the whole anchor corpus of this instance (7 live subscriptions, 30 days, 6 634 anchors with a weekly reset): **every identity has exactly ONE weekly reset phase** (`resetsAt mod 604800`), stable across the entire period, and **the seven phases are all distinct**. A window ROLL adds exactly one week, so the phase survives it; the ±60 s wobble between the `/usage` panel's spelling and the event stream's spelling of the SAME window (…340 vs …400) is normal and is what the ±120 s tolerance is for. So the response can be asked which credentials produced it — and that answer outranks the slot, the turn pin and the OTel observation, all of which are statements about what we BELIEVE the process is reading.

  **TWO RULES, both PURE in `src/reading-lag.js`.** ① **the LAG SHADOW** (`decideLagShadow`): after a re-point at T, a reading whose window matches the PREVIOUS slot's established window and NOT the new one is the previous slot's; the first reading that matches the NEW slot ends the shadow, and it stays ended (a later straggler is not evidence that the new credentials have not answered); when neither window decides — two members genuinely sharing a phase, or no established window yet — the rule falls through to the r3 statusline clause (*the link moved but the numbers did not*); and it is BOUNDED (10 min), so a session that never speaks again cannot pin a slot forever. It composes with the turn pin BEFORE the pin is set, so a pin created by a shadowed reading pins the PREVIOUS slot and the whole turn bills where its requests went. ② **the WINDOW IDENTITY GUARD** (`decideReadingTarget`, `guardReadingTarget` in the engine): wherever a reading is written for a member, a reading whose window contradicts that member's own established window is NEVER written there — re-filed when EXACTLY ONE account's window matches (identity groups collapsed, so `__global__` + its named sub are one account), else ARCHIVED to `data/archive/readings-window-mismatch.ndjson` with the reason, the target's own window and its age, plus telemetry and one journal line per session per verdict transition. **No evidence ⇒ no refusal**: a reading that states no window, and a target with no established window, are simply written.

  **THE ESTABLISHED WINDOW IS STAMPED AT THE WRITE, never read back out of `sevenDay.resetsAt`.** It is written by exactly ONE producer — `refreshViaCliPanel` (`claude -p /usage`), whose key and whose credential dir are the SAME decision (usage-routes says so in its own header). Inferring it from whatever the last write left in `sevenDay.resetsAt` would be circular: that field is precisely what a mis-filed reading overwrites, so one bad write would redefine the account and immunise every later one. **It lives in a SIDECAR, `data/usage-cache/.window-<key>` (`windowSidecarName`), not in the cache snapshot — see ROUND 2 (a) below for the reproduction that moved it.** `establishedWindows()` reads the sidecars keyed off the CACHE FILES, so a sidecar left behind by a removed account is invisible and can never become a re-file target; `captureRateLimitEvent` and `markLimitBanner` (both of which base their write on the identity group's FRESHEST sibling, and therefore used to have to rescue the window by hand) now have nothing to preserve and nothing to forget, and `reading-repair` seeds the sidecar while stripping any legacy in-snapshot copy.
