### src/window-targets.js — WINDOW TARGETS, SHARED (design-agent-browser-v2 §4.9 / §5.1.1 / §6.6; P9 first half, 2026-09-21)

  window-targets.js — node builtins + desktop-display only (the daemon can bundle it); every display-touching entry point takes `hostId` and refuses a non-local one by name. THE RULE IT ENCODES (D28): the agent talks to the TREE — AT-SPI2 is the native window's DOM — and to pixels only when the tree cannot answer. `snapshotTarget({pids, budget, text})` → `{snapshot, refs}`: the a11y tree of the applications whose pid ∈ pids with `@eN` minted in visit order (the agent-browser habit), the interface CENSUS every snapshot reports (§12.30: Action/EditableText/Text per node, buttons-with-Action — coverage is per toolkit and per desktop, never a constant), the `unreadable` subtrees, `truncated`, the timing. `refTableOf` keeps IDENTITY only (pid, path, role, name, bounds, actions, editable) — never the text; `resolveRef` refuses `ref_unknown` for anything not in the last snapshot. `actOnNode({entry, verb})` re-resolves the recorded path and the helper refuses `ref_stale` when the node there is no longer the one the ref named, `node_has_no_action` when a `do_action` lands on a node without `Action`, `node_not_editable` for text into a node without `EditableText`. `pickAction(actions, want)` = the preference `click > press > activate > doDefault > …`; Chromium/Electron put `showContextMenu` + `clickAncestor` on EVERY node (measured), so those and the `scroll*` family are NEVER picked unnamed (`--action` names one). `parseChord` is a CLOSED vocabulary (modifiers + one letter/digit/named key, spelled for xdotool) because the result reaches an argv — `ctrl+s; rm` is `bad_chord`, `ctrl++` is ctrl and the plus key, `ctrl+` is refused. `probeInputBackends({env, bins, ours})` = the RUNTIME ladder (§4.9 conclusion 2 — never a platform name): `xtest` (xdotool on OUR display; the only rung wired; a display that is not ours gets none — D27 (a)), `portal` (the RemoteDesktop portal on the session bus, `available:'consent'`, unwired — D29 (a)), `uinput` (a writable /dev/uinput, unwired, explicitly not recommended — D29 (b)); `injection` = the first row both available AND wired. `verbVerdicts({a11y, backends})` = §5.1.1's table PER VERB: `click`/`type`/`snapshot` ride the tree and are decided per NODE at act time; `key` and `click-at` exist only as injection and are refused WITH the probe rows when no wired backend exists; `screenshot` only from our display. `injectKey` (pointer moved into the window first — a bare Xvfb has PointerRoot focus — then `xdotool key --clearmodifiers <chord>`) and `injectClick` (`mousemove --sync x y click n`) are XTEST on our display; `screenshotDisplay` writes a PNG of a rectangle through the helper's Gdk op — the FALLBACK read.

  **THE TRAVERSAL NEVER RUNS ON THE EVENT LOOP.** `runHelper(req, {env, wallMs, python, helper})` spawns src/window-targets-helper.py with ONE JSON request on stdin, reads ONE JSON reply, keeps an `error` listener for life, SIGKILLs at `wallMs` and answers `helper_timeout` with the elapsed ms (the child is dead by then — suite §2), maps garbage to `helper_error` with the stderr tail, ENOENT to `python3_missing` naming the packages (python3-gi + gir1.2-atspi-2.0), a missing file to `helper_missing`, and any code outside `REFUSALS` to `helper_error` (+ `helperCode`) so a route never sees an unknown code. `TRAVERSAL_LIMITS` is the ONE home of the numbers: NODE_BUDGET 600 (default), SNAPSHOT_MAX_BUDGET 3000 (clamped), CALL_TIMEOUT_MS 800 (libatspi's per-method timeout inside the helper), WALL_MS 20 s (an unresponsive app costs one call timeout per node it owns, so the wall is what bounds it), ACT_WALL_MS 8 s, PROBE_MEMO_MS 60 s (a YES from the a11y / portal probes is remembered, a NO re-asked). `REFUSALS` is CLOSED and `refuse()` throws on a stranger; the routes' STATUS map must cover every member (suite §4 census).

  **P9 MEASUREMENTS (2026-09-21, this box: Ubuntu, GNOME Shell 50.1 on Wayland, xdg-desktop-portal 1.21.1 + -gnome 50.0, at-spi2 2.60.4, python 3.14.4, node 24.12 — the four things §10's P9 row said to measure FIRST; scripts/measure-window-targets.mjs reproduces them):**
  ① **The portal from a `systemd --user` background unit** (D29 / §12.29): from a transient `systemd-run --user` service — the same manager and context as vibespace.service — `RemoteDesktop.CreateSession` answered response 0 in 3 ms, `SelectDevices(types=7, persist_mode=2)` response 0, and `Start` raised the consent dialog (journal: "Failed to associate portal window with parent window", no Response within a 3 s wait; the session was Closed). So the public "portal/D-Bus is refused in background contexts" report does NOT hold here — the D-Bus path is open; what stands between a background service and injection is the USER'S click (§6.6), which nobody clicked in this measurement, so a granted background session is unproven. D29 (a) is viable; (c) stays the shipped state.
  ② **AT-SPI coverage on Chromium/Electron** (§12.30): LM Studio 0.3.32 (Electron) launched on our Xvfb with `--force-renderer-accessibility` — 357 nodes: Component 357/357, **Action 357/357** (`showContextMenu` on every node, `clickAncestor` 290, `press` 36, `doDefault` 13, `click` 11), **buttons with Action 43/43**, EditableText 0/357 (no field on that screen), Text 328/357. Every node has an action, which is not the same as every action being meaningful — hence `pickAction`'s never-by-default set. GTK3 (the fixture): 13 nodes, Action 3, EditableText 1, buttons with Action 2/2. gnome-shell (clutter/GJS, 600-node budget): Action 49/600, **74 buttons with 0 Action**. **Qt: NOT measured — no Qt toolkit is installed on this box**; the suite prints its own census so it can be re-read on a desktop that has one. Electron exported its tree only because the flag was passed; a keeper row for an Electron app should carry it (second half).
  ③ **`do_action` → UI change**: a GTK button, 30 clicks — the call itself median 0.08 ms, the tree-visible change (the label's new name read back through libatspi) median 0.34 ms, p95 0.81 ms, max 0.82 ms. Not measured on Electron (no known-safe widget to press in somebody's app).
  ④ **The node-side binding and its per-node cost** (§12.33): no maintained node AT-SPI binding exists (npm 2026-09-21: `@girs/atspi-2.0` / `@gi-types/atspi*` = GJS typings, `@girs/node-atspi-2.0` = typings for the native node-gtk, `dbus-next` 0.10.2 last modified 2022-04-28, two zero-history packages). Per-node cost is NOT what decides it — a cold walk costs the same order both ways: libatspi through python3 GI 600 gnome-shell nodes in 111–248 ms across four runs (2,400–5,400 nodes/s), the 357-node Electron tree in 78–81 ms (4,400–4,600 nodes/s); raw D-Bus with NO cache through Gio (up to 6 calls per node: GetRoleName, Name, GetInterfaces, GetExtents, GetActions, GetChildren) 0.34–0.51 ms/node = 1,970–2,900 nodes/s. The fork tax: helper spawn → probe reply 62–70 ms from a 47 MB node (+ the parent's RSS-proportional fork cost, §1.6's 72 ms at 1.5 GB), paid ONCE per traversal. Decision: python3 + GI in the bounded subprocess — the boundary is required by the event-loop law anyway, and a raw node client would be a dependency this repo does not carry for a cost it would not save.

  **P10 (2026-09-21):** `probeScreenCastPortal({env, bins, now})` — two read-only property Gets on the session bus (`ScreenCast.version`, `AvailableSourceTypes`, bit 2 = window sources), a YES memoised PROBE_MEMO_MS; it starts no session and raises no dialog (that is the user's click). The engine's desktop-class `screenshot` hands its answer to window-desktop's `captureVerdict`.

### src/window-desktop.js — TIER 3: THE USER'S REAL DESKTOP AS A WINDOW TARGET, PURE (design-agent-browser-v2 §7.6 / §7.1's `local-window` row / §4.9 columns 1-2 / §6.6, D27 (b) / D31; P10, 2026-09-21)

  window-desktop.js — imports nothing; the ONE model of the second window class the suite, the engine, the CLI and the browser registry all read. `ORIGINS` = `vibespace` (windows we started, D27 (a)) | `desktop` (the user's own desktop, D27 (b)); `SETTING_KEY` = `window.realDesktopTargets` (a `confirmOn` setting — the confirmation dialog IS the consent; agents cannot write settings, so the switch is a user act by construction); `consentVerdict({enabled})` admits exactly `true` (a string, a stale client copy, undefined = OFF, `desktop_consent_off` naming the switch); `desktopRows(a11yApps, {ourPids, selfPid})` = every application on the accessibility bus MINUS the keeper's pids and this process, `dw-<pid>` handles, every row `origin:'desktop'` + `yourDesktop:true` + `display:'your desktop'` — the AT-SPI desktop is the ONE enumeration road that holds in both §4.9 columns (measured: an Xwayland client and a native Wayland client both appear; only the first has an X window); `desktopVerbVerdicts` / `desktopActGate` = the class's law: `snapshot` / `click @ref` / `type @ref` ride the tree (`Action.do_action` / `EditableText`, NO injection), **`key` and `click --at` are refused BY NAME (`desktop_injection_refused`) whatever backend the display has** — a chord or a point on the real desktop lands in whatever has focus, possibly the window the user is typing in (§6.6); `watch` is `no_live_view` (the user is looking at it); `captureVerdict({sessionType, xWindow, ffmpeg, portal, display})` = §4.9 columns 1/2 decided PER WINDOW: an Xwayland client's own window through `x11grab -window_id` (its redirected pixmap — measured readable while the ROOT grabs black), a native Wayland window `capture_needs_portal` by name (ScreenCast v5, window sources; a consent click per session + persist_mode=2 + a PipeWire consumer, none wired), no DISPLAY / no ffmpeg / no window for the pid `capture_unavailable`. `TIER3_MEASUREMENTS` is THE RECORD of what §10's P10 row said to measure first (scripts/measure-tier3.mjs reproduces it; the local-oracles discipline: date, tool, box, a named status per column with a why, a refusal BY NAME where nothing was measured) and `WIRED` the rungs this version wires (`x11grabWindow`, `enumerateA11y`; NOT `portalScreenCast`, NOT `injection`); `measurementVerdict(rec, wired)` fails any WIRED claim whose evidence cell is not `ok` — a rung wired without re-measuring goes red (test-browser-tier3's negative controls). `hintAction(hint, {rowOf})` = what a §7.6 hint asks for: a tier-only hint is a SUGGESTION (`act:'open-window-target'` for 3, `switch-by-user` for 2, never `auto`), a backend hint DERIVES its tier from the row — nothing here ever performs a switch. The closed `REFUSALS` set (`desktop_consent_off`, `desktop_injection_refused`, `no_live_view`, `capture_needs_portal`, `capture_unavailable`, `desktop_window_gone`, `tier3_is_a_window_target`, `provider_needs_consent`, `escalation_needs_user`) is covered by routes/window-targets' STATUS (suite census).

### ssh-key-format.js

  ssh-key-format.js    — Private-key FORMAT classifier, PURE + shared server/browser (CJS pulled into the bundle like task-color-seq.js). **WHY a decoder and not a regex (2.246.0): an `openssh-key-v1` key's PEM armor is BYTE-IDENTICAL with or without a passphrase — the word ENCRYPTED appears NOWHERE** (only classic PEM's `Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED` and PKCS#8's `BEGIN ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY` announce themselves). The old first-3-lines /ENCRYPTED/ check therefore missed effectively every key produced since OpenSSH 7.8: they imported "fine" and failed at connect with a bare `Permission denied (publickey)` that never mentions a passphrase at ANY -v level. Encryption state lives in the DECODED body (`magic | ciphername | kdfname`; none/none = plain). classifyPrivateKey → {format: empty|openssh-v1|pkcs8|pem|ppk|ssh2|unknown, encrypted, cipher?, usable, malformed?}; TOTAL (runs on every keystroke — bounded to the first 256 base64 chars, length words capped at 64, hostile input returns a verdict and NEVER throws). ssh.com armor is FOUR dashes with spaces (`---- BEGIN SSH2 …----`), not the PEM five

### ssh-key.js

  ssh-key.js           — Server-side private-key UNLOCK at import (2.246.0). prepareImportedKey(text, passphrase) → {body, wasEncrypted, format, fingerprint, type}, KeyError codes key-encrypted/key-bad-passphrase/key-ppk/key-unsupported/key-not-a-key/key-too-large/key-no-ssh-keygen/key-unlock-unavailable/key-unlock-failed (the CLIENT renders localized text off the code). **PASSPHRASE TRANSPORT IS ENV, NEVER ARGV**: ssh-keygen reads a passphrase only from a tty or SSH_ASKPASS (never stdin), so a throwaway 0700 helper (`printf %s "$VIBESPACE_KEY_PASS"`) in a 0700 mkdtemp dir is exec'd with the secret in the CHILD ENV (/proc/<pid>/environ is 0400) + SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE=force; argv is only `-p -N '' -f <tmpfile>` (/proc/<pid>/cmdline is world-readable — the 2.126.0 rule) and HOME points at the temp dir so ssh-keygen can never touch the server's ~/.ssh. Temp dir removed on EVERY path incl. throws. **NON-NEGOTIABLE ERROR ORDER: an askpass helper that can't be exec'd (noexec tmpdir) makes ssh-keygen exit 255 saying "incorrect passphrase supplied" for a CORRECT passphrase — the only discriminator is the `ssh_askpass:` marker in stderr, which MUST be checked BEFORE the passphrase branch** or a hardened container lies to users forever. Fingerprint is computed in JS from the `-y` blob (byte-identical to `ssh-keygen -l`, verified — no extra spawn). node crypto is NOT an option: it cannot parse openssh-key-v1 at all, so a crypto-based impl passes RSA tests and fails every real ed25519 key. **The STORED key is UNLOCKED — this removes the passphrase, it does not preserve it** (every ssh here is BatchMode=yes and can never prompt); disclosed in docs/device-agent.md. Tests: scripts/test-ssh-key.mjs (60) + scripts/test-ssh-key-dialog.mjs (24, real headless browser)

### ctx-sync.js

  ctx-sync.js          — **THE ctx-folder sync, ONE implementation for every machine (2.277.0).** The old split — ssh=bidirectional rsync NO caps, dial=hashed sync with a SILENT ≤400-files/≤2MB cap — meant a 3MB context file reached every ssh host and never reached a dial device, invisibly. Hashed newer-wins sync (sha-equal ⇒ untouched, echo can't ping-pong; traversal-guarded pulls) over the device link on EVERY transport; ssh degrades to its legacy rsync pair only when the link is down; caps 1000 files/16MB and **every capped skip is REPORTED** (deduped serverNotice — a bounded sync may refuse a file, never lose one silently). Local sessions read the contextDir directly (TRANSPORT-ONLY, not a divergence). Test: scripts/test-ctx-sync.mjs (13).

### cli-identity.js

  cli-identity.js      — **THE agent-CLI process identity — ONE rule, two spellings (B-3185 r3).** "Is pid N the `claude`/`codex` CLI?" is asked by three consumers that used to answer it three ways: the pre-resume WRITER SWEEP (shell — decides who receives a SIGTERM), the ssh discovery **CO leg** (shell, the same text embedded verbatim — decides which codex threads read RUNNING) and **src/discovery-facts.js in JavaScript** (the local listing, the device snapshot's lock scan and its CO lines). B-3185 r1/r2 replaced the substring rule with an EXECUTABLE test in the two shell copies and RECORDED the JS one as a deliberate twin, on the grounds that it only labels a card RUNNING. r3 killed it: the blast radius genuinely differs, but a rule with two spellings has two behaviours the moment either is touched, and the loose spelling was doing real damage of its own — measured on the dev box, `cmdline.includes('claude')` answered YES for **106 of 4277 processes** against **16 real claude CLIs** (dtach masters, chat-wrappers, the generated `code` editor helper, a zsh shell-snapshot), and `isCodexCommandLine` for **30 against 4**, so any lock file whose pid had been RECYCLED by one of them produced exactly the phantom "running" session the PID-reuse guard exists to prevent. Exports `isCliProcess(pid, name)` (JS) + `cliIdentityShellFns()` (the POSIX `vs_argv`/`vs_is_cli` text, re-exported by writer-sweep.js so existing call sites are unchanged — the suite asserts it is the SAME function object, not a copy). **THE RULE, three rungs, one per shape the CLIs ship in:** ① argv[0]'s basename is the CLI name (`~/.local/bin/claude`; the codex vendor binary); ② argv[0] is an interpreter (node/nodejs/node.exe/bun/deno) and its FIRST NON-FLAG operand is the entry point (`node <prefix>/bin/claude`, `node …/@anthropic-ai/claude-code/cli.js`, `node …/@openai/codex/bin/codex.js`; up to 6 leading flags skipped); ③ `/proc/<pid>/exe` basename IS the CLI, or the exe is the native install's version FILE (`…/<name>/versions/<ver>`) **and** the process still PRESENTS as the CLI (argv[0] basename starts with the name, or argv[0] basename EQUALS the exe basename = nothing renamed) — the r2 narrowing that keeps a re-exec'd bundled helper (argv[0] `ugrep`, same image) out. A later ARGUMENT never identifies a process; that is exactly what the retired rule got wrong. **` (deleted)` IS STRIPPED FROM /proc/<pid>/exe (r3, defect 2).** The kernel appends it once the image is replaced on disk — which is what `claude` auto-update and `npm i -g @openai/codex` do to LIVE sessions; two of the four running agent CLIs on this box carry the suffix at any given moment. Without the strip BOTH executable rungs miss (basename `claude (deleted)`; the "nothing renamed" disjunct compares `2.1.258` against `2.1.258 (deleted)`), so the ONE process the sweep exists to stop — a mid-update CLI still appending to the transcript — survived it, and a double-writer is *most* likely right after an update lands. **argv IS A LIST OF NUL-SEPARATED WORDS AND A WORD MAY CONTAIN A NEWLINE (r4).** The JS side reads that list; the shell side could not, so `vs_argv` turned NULs into newlines and took the Nth LINE — which is the FIRST LINE of the Nth word. The two spellings therefore answered differently about the same live process whenever a word carried a newline, in BOTH directions and both harmful: argv[0] `/usr/bin/claude<LF>/usr/bin/tail` is basename `tail` to JS and `claude` to the old shell (the sweep SIGTERMs a reader — B-3185's own harm through a different door), and `<dir>/dir<LF>name/claude` is the reverse (a real writer survives the sweep, which is the double-writer the sweep exists to prevent). The shell now parks real newlines on `\001` for the line select and restores them after (`tr '\n' '\001' | tr '\0' '\n' | sed -n Np | tr '\001' '\n'`), so "the Nth line" IS "the Nth NUL-record" in either spelling; the residue is a literal `\001` inside an argv word coming back as a newline — a byte no path or flag carries, and since the swap cannot move a `/` the basename splits at the same place in both spellings, so it can only make a word look LESS like the CLI. The `ps` fallback flattens its blob first (`tr '\n' ' '`) because the JS twin's `/\s+/` split always treated a newline as a space while awk splits per line. **THAT LAST SENTENCE WAS A DESCRIPTION UNTIL r5.** The `ps` branch is the NO-/proc rung (macOS/BSD ssh hosts); on a Linux box every fixture takes the /proc rung, so the half of the r4 fix that lives there shipped with no assertion and no control — (r) again. It is now DRIVEN, with no edit to the text under test: the `/proc/$1/` root is re-rooted so BOTH reads miss (three literals, asserted — leaving the exe read live let rung 3 decide and the `ps` rung was never reached), a stand-in `ps` sits first on PATH, and the JS twin runs in a child whose two /proc reads THROW so the shipped `procArgv`/`isCliProcess` really take their own fallback. The stand-in is asserted to be necessary rather than assumed: measured, procps 4.x `ps -o args=` renders an embedded newline as a SPACE, so this box's own `ps` cannot produce the multi-line blob the flattening exists for. Both spellings must return the identical word for argv[0..2] and the identical verdict on three live fixtures (`ps` cannot recover word boundaries — fixture `…/claude<LF>/usr/bin/tail` is `claude` to BOTH here while the /proc rung calls it `tail`; that is a property of `ps`, not a divergence); negative control = the verbatim pre-r4 line without the flattening, which makes awk print field i of EVERY line and answers the OPPOSITE of the JS twin on both newline fixtures while staying indistinguishable on a plain one. **AND THE VALUE STILL HAD TO SURVIVE `$(…)`, WHICH STRIPS EVERY TRAILING NEWLINE (r4, second half — found by measuring the r4 fix instead of describing it).** A word or path that ENDS in one read `…/claude` in the shell and `…/claude<LF>` in JS, i.e. the shell said YES where THE identity says NO, on the paths that kill. All three captures were affected and each needed its own live fixture: argv[0] `…/claude<LF>` (rung 1), argv[0] `…/claude<0x01>` (the park byte comes back out AS a newline, so a TRAILING one was eaten too — that is the one case where the residue sentence above would have been false), and `/proc/<pid>/exe` `…/claude<LF>` under a launcher argv[0] (rung 3, unreachable from any argv fixture). One helper, `vs_cap <cmd> <args…>`, captures all three: a sentinel byte appended INSIDE the subshell protects the tail, then exactly ONE terminator — the one `sed`/`awk`/`readlink` printed itself — comes off (`vs_c_v` is the out-parameter; POSIX has no nameref). Gate: two live fixtures for the mid-word half (one per direction) with the pre-r4 `vs_argv` reader as the negative control (it answers the OPPOSITE of the JS twin on both), three for the trailing half with the three pre-`vs_cap` `$(…)` captures as the negative control (it answers YES to all three, and is proven not-dead on a normal claude / a `tail`), all five in the cross-login-shell verdict matrix (`${v%"$nl"}` is the same quoted-pattern construct the `(deleted)` strip got wrong under zsh) and in the JS⇄shell parity matrix. Reverting `vs_cap` in the product turns five asserts red. **THE SHELL TEXT RUNS UNDER THE REMOTE LOGIN SHELL, NOT `sh` (r3 round 2).** The device rung runs it as `sh -c`, but BOTH ssh rungs — the sweep's fallback (`sweepWriters`) and the discovery CO leg (`hosts.js _ssh`) — hand the script to `ssh host -- <script>`, which the REMOTE USER'S LOGIN SHELL interprets, so "POSIX sh" is the floor and not the target. This bit the `(deleted)` strip on arrival: in zsh `(…)` is a glob GROUP, so the unquoted `${vs_c_e% (deleted)}` matched " deleted" and stripped NOTHING — the auto-update fix was dead on every zsh-login host (a very common default) and invisible to a suite whose every identity assertion ran `sh -c`. The pattern is QUOTED (`${vs_c_e%' (deleted)'}`), which POSIX makes literal in every shell (verified dash/bash/busybox/zsh/ksh). **Quote any pattern whose literal characters are special somewhere, and test embedded shell text under every shell that can interpret it.** Gated functionally: test-writer-sweep drives the SHIPPED text through every login shell present on the box against the live `(deleted)` fixtures and demands identical verdicts, with the UNQUOTED spelling as the negative control — it parses and is indistinguishable under `sh`, and diverges only under zsh. **Dependency-free on purpose** (node builtins only): the agentd bundle carries discovery-facts, so it now carries this too — the arch suite's SHARED tier holds the line. Parity is FUNCTIONAL, not hoped for: scripts/test-writer-sweep.mjs §6 drives both spellings over ~18 live fixture pids × both CLI names in the same instant (with a not-vacuous check that the matrix contains both verdicts, and the retired JS rule as the negative control that a divergence really does turn it red), and scripts/test-discovery-interpret.mjs §8 does the same on the discovery side (real `bin/claude`/`bin/codex` holders, a `tail -f` reader, a wrapper that merely NAMES the codex binary in its arguments while holding an inherited rollout fd). **AND THE `lsof` RUNGS ARE THE SAME RULE TOO (r3).** Every consumer has a no-/proc body for macOS/BSD, and being unreachable from Linux is how BOTH of them kept the retired identity after the /proc bodies were fixed: discovery-facts' rung asked `/codex/.test(cmd)` (lsof's COMMAND field = comm, a SUBSTRING) and the hosts.js CO leg's `else` asked `awk … c ~ /codex/`. Worse, r1/r2 emitted the shared shell functions INSIDE that leg's `then` block, so `vs_is_cli` did not even EXIST in the branch that needed it — they now sit above the `if`. Both rungs emit `-Fpn` (pid + name) and credit the pid through the shared predicate. Gate: test-writer-sweep §9 RUNS the CO leg's else-branch by substituting ONE literal (the `[ -d /proc/self ]` probe), with the verbatim pre-r3 awk as the negative control (a `codex-keeper`-only rollout reported RUNNING), and §12 pins `-Fpn`/no-`c ~ /codex/` plus the definitions-before-the-`if` ordering. **A branch no test can reach is a branch that drifts; make it reachable by substituting one literal rather than by trusting it.** **AND IT NOW ALSO OWNS THE EXISTENCE PROBE — `pidAliveShellFn()`, `vs_alive <pid>` (B-3185 r6).** "Does this pid exist?" is the question that comes BEFORE identity, it runs on the same three transports under the same floor (`sh -c` on the device rung, the REMOTE USER'S LOGIN SHELL on both ssh rungs — so busybox `ash` is real), and it had TWO spellings: r5 fixed `hosts.js killPidShell` and left `src/server/sysinfo-wiring.js signalProc` its own `ps -p` on a written reason, which described only ONE of that script's two `ps -p` calls. The other — the post-signal aliveness check on the SUCCESS branch — MANUFACTURED a false `{ok:true, gone:true}` under busybox for a process that ignored the SIGTERM (measured). The ladder is now emitted from here and embedded by both: `kill -0` (POSIX builtin everywhere; SUCCESS is proof, FAILURE is ambiguous between EPERM and ESRCH so it is handed DOWN, never believed) → `[ -d /proc/N ]` → `ps -p N` (the no-/proc rung). No JS twin on purpose: the local branches call `process.kill(pid,0)` and read `e.code`, which is the errno distinction the shell cannot make and the whole reason the ladder exists. **A twin kept alive by a comment is a twin — the comment is only as good as its author's count of the call sites**, so the guard is a STANDING SWEEP (test-writer-sweep §17) rather than a better sentence: no `ps -p` may be an EXISTENCE test on any kill/signal path, each surviving one is allowlisted WITH its reason, and a dead entry fails too. **r7: that sweep was itself gated on a hand-written seven-file list** — the same instrument the bug had already defeated three times, enforcing the rule only where its author had looked (measured: 47 real signal-sending files were outside it, including `server.js`, `jobs.js`, `boot-restore.js`, `plugins/vnc/port-forward/opencode-serve`, `agentd.js`, `ws-handler/ws-create`). The set is now DERIVED by grep — every non-test file under `src/`, `data/bin/`, `scripts/` and the repo ROOT whose text sends or probes a signal, extension-less tools entering by SHEBANG so a GENERATED (untracked) agent CLI is reached at all — the suite PRINTS what it walked, the grep is deliberately over-inclusive (a false positive only widens enforcement; a false negative is the defect), the shipped sweep is parameterised by ROOT and re-run against a temp tree carrying each shape as its controls, and every exported shell BUILDER is swept on the text it EMITS (a source scan cannot see a runtime-composed probe). GENERATED files (gitignored — the esbuild daemon bundle carries cli-identity's `ps -p` lines verbatim, so a rebuilt tree went red on a CLEAN checkout) are a THIRD bucket with a stricter rule that needs no author: every `ps -p` line in them must be VERBATIM in an authored file the sweep walked. **A standing sweep is only as good as the set it walks: derive the set from the property, never enumerate it, and print what was walked.** **THE {uid, argv} VALUE READ LIVES HERE TOO (B-eac2 residual (c)).** `readPsIdentity(pid, {execImpl, now})` — /proc first (zero fork), `ps -p <pid> -o uid=,args=` where there is no /proc (macOS is "full support" in the README and has no procfs, so a procfs-only reader answers `null` for EVERY pid there), ONE call carrying both facts, memoised per pid for `PS_IDENTITY_TTL_MS` (1s) because its two readers `procCmdline`/`procUid` always ask about the same pid back to back. It was the FOURTH spelling of this ladder — src/opencode-serve.js's keeper carried its own, and that keeper `killPid`s — so it moved to the module where the rule already lives and the keeper requires it. **It is a VALUE read, never an existence probe**: an unanswerable `ps` yields `null`, which every caller reads as "no evidence" (classifyRecordedPid turns it into the verdicts that REFUSE to signal), and `kill -0` — `pidAliveShellFn` / `process.kill(pid,0)` — stays the only thing that decides whether a process is there. `ps` renders argv as ONE blob, so a caller may ASK this answer questions (`serve`, `--port <n>`) and may never reconstruct a command from it. THE ONE COPY: `data/bin/vibespace-opencode-op` keeps a parity twin because a checkout-less ssh host cannot require this module — the same documented exception as the shipped usage scanner — and scripts/test-opencode-remote.mjs drives both over the same inputs, including the memoisation rule. **The standing sweep now sees this line at all**: `ps -p` has two spellings and only one of them is a string — shell writes `ps -p "$1"`, JS writes `execFileSync('ps', ['-p', …])` where the flag and the program never touch — so §17's claim silently excluded every JS caller until `namesPsP` learned the argv form. Widening it surfaced SIX pre-existing JS reads (agentd lstart/command, session-store ppid ×2 and the `comm=` twin, and procArgv's own no-/proc rung); each is a value read and now carries its reason in `PS_P_ALLOWED`, with a negative control (a JS existence probe next to a kill is caught) and a positive one (`execFileSync("psql", ["-p", …])` is not — the pattern names the PROGRAM, so it does not make every `-p` flag owe a reason). **2026-09-14 增 THE SESSION TABLE** (the desktop-app keeper's r2): `readSid(pid)` (stat field 6, from the last `)`), `sessionIndex({procRoot, now, fresh})` (Map sid → pids, ONE /proc walk memoised PROC_TABLE_TTL_MS, `fresh` rebuilds now — a caller judging a pid it spawned since the last walk may not read a memo) and `sessionMembers(sid, opts)`; a detached leader's sid is its own pid, so this is the census a keeper needs to stop an application WITH the children it forked, to sample what the whole application burns, and to verify a listening socket's owner. VALUE reads: no /proc ⇒ empty = no evidence; deliberately NO `ps` rung (desktop apps are a /proc-machine feature in v1, and a rung no test can reach is prose). Gate: test-desktop-display §4. **2026-09-14 (desktop keeper r3): `procSample` also returns `reapedTicks` = cutime+cstime (stat fields 16+17) — the work of every child the process has WAITED for; which ticks a guard SUMS is the consumer's rule: desktop-display.sessionSample counts own+reaped over a SET (each unit of work once), opencode-serve keeps `cpuTicks` for its ONE pid (a lone parent's cutime arrives as a lifetime lump when a long-lived child exits — a spike, not a rate).**

  **THE PROCESS TREE IS READ HERE TOO, AND WITHOUT FORKING (2026-09-09, userW's pod).** `readPpid` (`/proc/<pid>/stat` field 4, counted from the LAST `)` because comm may hold spaces AND parens — the same rule `procStartTicks` uses for field 22) and `readChildPids` (the union of `/proc/<pid>/task/<tid>/children`, because children are recorded against the THREAD that forked them) joined the identity rule because they are the same kind of fact, read from the same place, and the answer must not depend on which caller asks. They replace the discovery sweep's `ps -p <pid> -o ppid=` PER LOCK and `pgrep -P <childPid>` PER LIVE SESSION. **THE COST WAS NEVER THE WAIT, IT IS THE FORK**: `execFile` is asynchronous about the wait, while fork(2)/posix_spawn copies the CALLING process's page tables on the calling thread — measured in a plain node process on the dev box, one `spawn('true')`: **1.8 ms at 45 MB RSS, 18.8 ms at 543 MB, 67-73 ms at 1.5 GB** — and `Promise.all` lines N of them up inside ONE tick, so 2.242.0's sync→async fix moved the blocking without removing it. The no-/proc rung (macOS/BSD, where "full support" is a README promise) is **ONE `ps -eo pid=,ppid=` for the WHOLE SWEEP** (`parentIndex`, memoised `PROC_TABLE_TTL_MS` = 2 s, deliberately under the /api/sessions cache's own 4.5 s so consecutive sweeps re-read rather than reason about a stale table) — never one exec per pid, which is the shape being retired. `hasProcfs` remembers a YES for good and re-checks a NO every 60 s (the opencode `hostCanIdentify` law: one failed stat must not become permanent degradation to forking). Every one of them is a VALUE read, never an existence probe — an answer nobody can give is `null` / `[]` = "no evidence", and `kill -0` remains the only thing allowed to say a pid is gone. `procRoot` is injectable so the no-/proc rungs can be DRIVEN on Linux (the r5 `vs_argv` lesson: a rung no test can reach is prose). Gate: scripts/test-discovery-spawn.mjs + the §45 build census in test-architecture. **r2: `readChildPids` has a SECOND consumer and it is the hotter one** — server.js's `refreshWebuiPids()` runs on every kill IN-BAND and 3 s after every create, where the `pgrep -P` it replaces cost **9,180.6 ms of blocked loop for 61 sessions at 1,560 MB RSS** against **2.3 ms** here, for the identical 244 pids. That is why this reader lives beside the identity rule rather than inside the sweep: the same fact, one implementation, and the module that asks it is a parameter. **r3: the LAST fork on the kill path came here too.** `pidsMatchingCmdline(needle)` answers `pgrep -f`'s question — "which live pids carry this string in their command line" — for the ONE caller that asks it, ws-handler's kill case looking for the dtach master that owns a session's socket. /proc rung: every `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` read into ONE reused 64 KiB buffer (a read that FILLS it re-reads that pid whole, so a giant argv is answered rather than silently truncated), byte-compared with `Buffer.indexOf` so nothing is decoded per pid; no-/proc rung: ONE `pgrep -f` for the WHOLE question, never one per candidate. It is `async` because that fallback must stay async — a Mac pays the fork too, and making it synchronous to keep one signature would be a regression. **Matching is a literal byte substring where `pgrep -f`'s is an ERE, i.e. STRICTLY NARROWER** — the safe direction for a caller that SIGTERMs what it finds, and it cannot miss the real holder, whose argv carries the path verbatim; a needle containing a SPACE is matched against the space-joined form because /proc separates argv words with NUL, while a space-free needle must lie inside one argv word and needs no normalisation (verified against `pgrep -f` on real processes for all three: /proc rung, no-/proc rung, and a needle spanning two argv words). **The trade is different from readPpid's and is stated rather than implied**: this scan is FLAT in the server's own size (23.6-23.7 ms, 3,400 processes) while the fork it replaces is not (2.0 ms of blocked loop at 58 MB, 24.4 ms at 559 MB, 69.4 ms at 1,564 MB; end to end 87.6/110.6/155.2 ms) — so at the shape the incident was reported on it is 69 ms of block down to 24 and 155 ms of latency down to 24, and the honest cost is a freshly booted 58 MB server paying 24 ms of block where a fork was 2. Gate: test-discovery-spawn §9 drives the SHIPPED kill-path body sliced out of ws-handler with a fake `process` that RECORDS SIGTERMs instead of sending them, over three real processes carrying the needle, with `git show master:src/ws-handler.js`'s copy as the negative control on the same fixture (0 spawns / 23.6 ms vs 1 spawn / 84 ms, the IDENTICAL pid set, the session's own attach pty excluded).

### discovery-facts.js

  discovery-facts.js   — **Shared discovery INTERPRETATION (2.278.0)** — deliberately tiny so the esbuild agentd bundle carries it (unlike the ssh one-file scanner, the daemon CAN share code). Parity in test-usage-scan-op: device-computed claims BYTE-IDENTICAL to the server-side interpretation of the same snapshot. Original note: — the ~120-line lock-first CLAIM algorithm (exact-id → tail-id → mtime; keeper adoption; codex rollout cards; brand-new-lock case) extracted verbatim out of hosts.discoverSessions so the interpretation can run WHERE the facts live (the future dark `discovery.v2` op — device computes its own claims, orchestrator only merges). `claimJsonls` INJECTED (session-store must not be pulled into this tiny module). Golden-fixture parity: scripts/test-discovery-interpret.mjs (18 — the 9 tricky claim cases + §8, the process-identity twin: wiring pin, the PID-reuse guard on real processes with the retired rule as the negative control, the CO-line scan, and JS⇄shell parity over the same live pids). Fixture trap recorded in the m3m4 suite: /bin/sleep can be a uutils MULTI-CALL binary that dispatches on argv0 — a symlink named 'claude' dies; use a script. ### writer-sweep.js

  writer-sweep.js      — **THE pre-resume writer sweep, ONE implementation for every machine (CS separation, 2.276.0).** The invariant: before resuming, no OTHER process may still be writing that conversation's transcript (two writers on one JSONL = the B-4058 corruption class). It used to exist THREE times — ssh, dial, and NOT AT ALL for local; the local gap was never a decision, it is what happens when `hostId` is a BRANCH instead of a PARAMETER (whoever fixes the remote bug never exercises the local twin). `sweepWriters(hosts, hostId, rid, …)` — falsy hostId = this machine via device #0; ssh keeps its per-op channel as fallback, dial correctly has none, local throws rather than pretending. Every kill leg echoes `SWEPT:<pid>` and the created reply carries them (a destructive op must never be silent). **FORKS NEVER SWEEP (2.284.4, real incident: forking a LIVE conversation SIGTERMed the parent's claude mid-turn the day the local sweep went live)** — a fork resumes the PARENT's rid but only READS that transcript and writes a NEW id's JSONL, so a live parent writer is legitimate; the resume-already-live guard exempts forks by design, which voids the "live sessions were filtered upstream" assumption the sweeps were written under. All three ws-handler gates carry `!data.fork`; the test's drift guard fails any new call site without it. Test: scripts/test-writer-sweep.mjs. **CODEX LEGS (P1 codex double-writer, 2026-09).** `writerSweepScript(rid, shq, {backend, protectSids})` / `sweepWriters(…, {backend, protectSids})`: the claude script is byte-for-byte what it was (default backend); `backend:'codex'` swaps the holder legs for ① a /proc fd scan (lsof on macOS/BSD) for an open `rollout-*-<threadId>.jsonl` — the pattern also matches `.jsonl.zst` (codex ≥0.153 may compress) — and ② an argv leg for `codex resume <threadId>` (a TUI in an external terminal) / `CODEX_WEBUI_RESUME_ID=<threadId>` (an orphaned VibeSpace wrapper or its dtach master); the pipe-session-meta + keeper legs are shared. Both codex legs report `SWEPT:`; the fd leg's holder must pass `vs_is_cli <pid> codex` (the EXECUTABLE test below — the pre-B-3185 text said "kill only `*codex*` cmdlines", which is the substring rule the fix retired), and the argv leg is deliberately exempt because it is self-evidencing. **THE PROTECT LIST is load-bearing**: a codex app-server keeps EVERY rollout of its thread tree open for its whole lifetime — measured on the dev box, one app-server (`…/bin/codex app-server`) held the parent + three finished sub-agent rollouts two days later — so a plain "kill the holder" would SIGTERM a healthy LIVE session's app-server whenever a sub-agent or forked-away thread is resumed (the 2.284.4 class). ws-create's `sweepOpts(hostId)` passes the webui ids of the live codex sessions on the TARGET machine; the script resolves a candidate's `CLAUDE_WEBUI_SESSION_ID` from its argv (dtach/wrapper carry the env pairs as args) or `/proc/<pid>/environ` (`ps -E` on macOS) and skips protected holders — live sessions are the resume-already-live guard's business, the sweep reaches EXTERNAL/orphaned writers only. The argv leg scans `ps -eo pid=,args=`, and the sweep's own `sh -c <script>` carries RID in its argv: the literal `VS_WRITER_SWEEP` sentinel in the script text is what skips the sweep shell and its subshells — keep it. Protect ids are validated `^[\w-]+$` before they reach the shell. Parity: local and remote receive a byte-identical codex script (test §8); test §9 drives the real script against real holder processes (temp HOME, real rollout path shape, SIGTERM observed; protect-list positive/negative; argv leg; .zst; non-codex holder untouched; the claude script never touches a codex holder); test §10 pins the ws-create guard functionally (real `createWsCreateHandler`) + every sweep site passing `sweepOpts`. **IDENTITY IS THE EXECUTABLE, NOT A SUBSTRING OF THE COMMAND LINE (B-3185).** The holder test used to be `case "$(ps -p $pid -o args=)" in *claude*)` — a substring over the WHOLE command line — so every process whose argv merely NAMED a path under `~/.claude` read as the CLI and was SIGTERMed: `tail -f ~/.claude/projects/<id>.jsonl`, an editor with the transcript open, and (the first casualty, patched around IN THE SUITE for a while instead of fixed) a test process running from a git worktree under `~/.claude/worktrees/` — where the worktree-only-smokes law puts every agent — which matched its own guard and killed itself: exit 143, `npm run ci` red, on code that was fine. `vs_is_cli <pid> <claude|codex>` (cliIdentityShellFns — **which lives in src/cli-identity.js since r3 and is only RE-EXPORTED here, beside its JS twin `isCliProcess`; read that entry**) now decides by the EXECUTABLE, in three rungs covering the three shapes the CLIs actually ship in: argv[0]'s basename (`~/.local/bin/claude`; the codex vendor binary `…/@openai/codex-linux-x64/vendor/<triple>/bin/codex` that the npm `codex.js` shim spawns by path), the interpreter's FIRST NON-FLAG operand when argv[0] is node/nodejs/bun/deno (`node <prefix>/bin/claude` via the npm shebang shim, `node …/@anthropic-ai/claude-code/cli.js`, `node …/bin/codex.js`), and `/proc/<pid>/exe` (a native install execs `~/.local/share/claude/versions/<ver>` behind an argv[0] of `~/.local/bin/claude`). argv is read NUL-split out of `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` where that exists (exact) and falls back to `ps -o args=` word splitting elsewhere, and a trailing ` (deleted)` is stripped from `/proc/<pid>/exe` before either exe rung matches (**r3**: the kernel appends it when the image is replaced on disk — what auto-update does to a LIVE session — and without the strip the sweep missed exactly the mid-update CLI it exists to stop). Only argv[0] and the first non-flag operand are ever consulted — a later ARGUMENT never identifies a process, which is exactly what the old rule got wrong. THE FD EVIDENCE STAYS PRIMARY (the process holds THIS conversation's transcript open); vs_is_cli only answers writer-or-reader. THE ARGV LEG IS DELIBERATELY EXEMPT: `codex resume <threadId>` / `CODEX_WEBUI_RESUME_ID=<threadId>` is self-evidencing (it names the thread) and the shape it catches — an orphaned VibeSpace wrapper or its dtach master — is NOT the codex binary, so `vs_codex_kill` keeps only the PROTECT check and each caller supplies its own evidence. **THE FD SCAN IS BATCHED — AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE (B-3185).** `fdScanShellFns()` emits `vs_fd_scan <ere>` (one `<pid>\t<fd target>` line per matching open fd) + `vs_fd_pids`; both backend scripts embed it VERBATIM, and `src/server/boot-restore.js` builds its "which conversations does a live claude still hold?" probe from the same export (same scan, kill removed). Measured on the dev box (32 cores, loadavg 3.4–4.8, 3678–3713 processes, 405,735 open fds): the old per-process `ls` + `grep` fork PAIR = 7356 forks, 9.9–12.2 s wall — over half the 20 s budget spent on fork/exec alone, and past it entirely on a busier or bigger machine; the batched form (one `ls -l` per 400 fd directories + one awk) = ~20 forks, 3.0–3.5 s, so the UNCHANGED 20 s budget now covers ~24k processes. boot-restore's variant was worse and silently dead: a `readlink` fork PER FD (~6.4 minutes here) against a 6 s timeout it therefore ALWAYS blew, swallowed by a bare catch — every local conversation looked "not live" and the socket dedup fell back to createdAt; it now runs the shared scan and a failure LOGS. Two shell facts are load-bearing: `/proc/self/fd` rides in every chunk so `ls -l` always has more than one operand and therefore always prints the `<dir>:` headers the pid attribution reads (with a single operand it prints none), and the scan is CHUNKED because `vs_fd_chunk` EXECS `ls`: ITS argv is one operand per process and is what ARG_MAX/MAX_ARG_STRLEN bound, and an E2BIG there fails into a discarded stderr and a silently empty answer. **The old boot probe's `/proc/[0-9]*/fd/*` glob was NOT an ARG_MAX case** (r1's comment said it was, and the r2 review caught it): a shell `for` loop expands in the shell's own memory and never reaches execve — its problem was only the 405,735 `readlink` forks. Naming the wrong mechanism in a comment is how the next person removes the right guard, so both copies and both kb twins are pinned by the suite. Next rung if a machine ever needs it: GNU `find -lname` measures 0.76 s — not adopted, because it is not portable and 3 s is inside budget. **WHICH LEG ACTUALLY REACHES A LIVE CLAUDE (measured, and it changes how you read the fix):** the installed CLI (2.1.226, native binary) does NOT keep the transcript open — it appends and closes; a machine-wide scan of this box found ZERO processes holding any `~/.claude/projects/**.jsonl` while 16 claude CLIs were running. So the claude FD leg is a rung that fires for a holder that happens to exist — an older CLI, a mid-append race, or a READER — while the leg that really catches a live claude is the CLI's own `~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json` lock file. That makes the old substring guard worse than it looks: the leg that almost never finds a real writer was the one matching every process that merely named a path under `~/.claude`. It also bounds boot-restore's probe honestly — it now runs correctly and fast, but it still answers "nobody" for current claude; giving `claudeAlive` the CLI registry (with the `procStart` counter-capture against pid reuse) is a separate decision, because retiring is destructive (SIGTERM + unlink the dtach socket). The CODEX fd leg is the live one: real app-servers on this box do hold their rollouts open, which is why the PROTECT list exists. Field-validated read-only against 3700 real processes: of 70 whose argv merely contains 'claude', exactly the 16 real CLIs answer yes and the dtach masters and chat-wrappers that carry the whole `…/claude --resume …` command line as ARGUMENTS answer no (the old rule said yes to all of them — and SIGTERMing a dtach master destroys the session); both real codex shapes (`node …/bin/codex app-server` through the npm shim and the `…/vendor/<triple>/bin/codex` binary) answer yes. Test §6 is now the identity matrix on real processes: WRITERS that must be swept (a native `…/bin/claude`, `node …/@anthropic-ai/claude-code/cli.js`, `node <prefix>/bin/claude`) and READERS that must survive (`tail -f` on the transcript — proven non-vacuous by checking its fd first — a process running from a `.claude/worktrees/` path, a `cli.js` outside a claude package, a neutral `node -e` holder, and THE SUITE'S OWN PROCESS holding the same fd, under a SIGTERM trap so a regression is a red assertion instead of a mysterious exit 143). §1 pins the batching structurally (exactly one `/proc/[0-9]*` walk per script, no per-process `ls`, no whole-argv identity test) and asserts that every `kill -TERM` line carries a `SWEPT:` — intent, not the old count, which the dedup would have broken. §11 pins the boot-restore wiring. **R2 REVIEW ROUND (six defects, each with a negative control).** ① The §1 drift pin was UNSATISFIABLE — its regex matched neither the exact pre-fix line nor any realistic reintroduction, so the kb advertised a guard that could never go red; the pin is now asserted against the verbatim pre-B-3185 lines AND proven by splicing them back into the shipped script. ② The awk pid attribution never cleared `p` on an UNRECOGNISED directory header — and `/proc/self/fd`, appended to every chunk by design, is exactly such a header AND is the `ls` process's own fd table, which inherits the sweeping shell's fds: an inherited matching fd was attributed to whichever numeric pid came last in the chunk, and the sweep SIGTERMs on that attribution. `p` is now reset on EVERY header; §1b proves it functionally (the shell holds the target on fd 9, so `ls` inherits it in every chunk) with the sticky-`p` revert as the control — one bogus victim per chunk. ③ The ARG_MAX rationale above. ④ RUNG 3 WAS A WIDENING INSIDE A NARROWING FIX: `*/<name>/versions/*` on `/proc/<pid>/exe` classified every process running the CLI's binary IMAGE as the CLI — and the CLI RE-EXECS that image as its bundled helpers (measured live: 18–19 processes under `…/share/claude/versions/<ver>`, 2–3 of them `ugrep -G …` with argv[0] a bare `ugrep`), so a search helper that inherited its parent's transcript fd was a SIGTERM target. Rung 3 now also asks how the process PRESENTS itself and takes either honest answer — argv[0] basename starts with `<name>` (a launcher naming the CLI), or argv[0] basename EQUALS the exe basename (nothing renamed: a wrapper's `exec "$IMG"`, the shape that keeps the rung reachable at all). A re-exec'd helper fails both because it renames itself. The measured real CLI never needs rung 3 (argv[0] is `~/.local/bin/claude`, so rung 1 answers) — which is why widening it was pure downside. §6 runs ONE binary under THREE argv[0]s (same `/proc/<pid>/exe`, asserted) and reverts rung 3 to r1 against the LIVE helper pid as the control. ⑤ The "SUITE ITSELF" leg labelled its argv from `process.argv[1]`, which node ABSOLUTISES, while the guard reads the command line AS TYPED — so it announced "the real regression shape" for a run whose argv contained no `.claude` at all. A COPY of the suite (holder mode, top of file) now runs from a real `.claude/worktrees/<wt>/scripts/` checkout BOTH ways — absolute (the argv that SIGTERMed the suite) and relative (what the gate types) — with the two argvs read out of `/proc` and asserted. ⑥ THE STANDING-SWEEP TWIN: hosts.js's remote-discovery `CO` leg still carried all three retired shapes (a `tr`+`grep` fork PAIR per process over `/proc/[0-9]*`, a `readlink` fork per FD, and an argv-regex identity) — measured on this box 5.02 s / 8068 forks at 4034 processes inside a per-host discovery budget, versus 3.52 s / ~20 forks for the ported leg. `codexOpenRolloutsShell()` (hosts.js) now embeds `fdScanShellFns()` + `cliIdentityShellFns()` VERBATIM, so the sweep and discovery answer "is this the codex CLI" identically by construction; §12 pins that structurally with the pre-B-3185 leg as the control, and §9 runs it for real (a wrapper/dtach-master that merely NAMES `…/bin/codex resume <tid>` in its ARGUMENTS is no longer a RUNNING thread — the retired regex says yes to it, asserted). **THE PORT ALSO EXPOSED A LIVE HAZARD THE SUITE CAUGHT: this leg is the LAST command of the ssh discovery script and `_ssh` REJECTS a non-zero exit, and a `while read` loop exits with its LAST iteration's status — so the leg returned 1 whenever the last matching fd under `$HOME` belonged to a non-CLI holder, sending the whole host's discovery into the serve-stale-cache catch. It ends in an explicit `:`; never let a scan's FINDINGS decide a script's exit status.** ⑦ The kb's advertised assert count is now self-checked by §13. **THAT TWIN IS GONE (r3 — the standing sweep is a MEASUREMENT, and "recorded" is not "resolved"):** r2 left `src/discovery-facts.js` identifying processes by command line — `pidLooksClaude` = `cmdline.includes('claude')`, `isCodexCommandLine` = a whole-argv regex — for the DEVICE snapshot's liveness labels, on the grounds that it only decides whether a card reads RUNNING and never who receives a SIGTERM. The blast radius really is different, and it was still the wrong call: a rule with two spellings has two behaviours the moment either is touched, and the loose spelling was doing its own damage (measured: YES for 106 of 4277 processes against 16 real claude CLIs; 30 vs 4 for codex — so a RECYCLED lock pid on any dtach master, chat-wrapper or editor helper produced the exact phantom the PID-reuse guard exists to prevent). Both now call `isCliProcess` from src/cli-identity.js. §12 still pins the boundary that must never be crossed (no kill path in discovery-facts or cli-identity — they classify; only the sweep script kills), and parity is now FUNCTIONAL on both sides (test-writer-sweep §6/§12, test-discovery-interpret §8) instead of a promise.

The `.meta` therefore records `remotePath` + `compressed` next to {size,mtime}: a changed path invalidates the slot (full refetch, no cache-valid short-circuit), and a compressed remote — or an already-compressed cache file (magic-byte check, so pre-fix metas are covered too) — is NEVER delta-appended, because recompression rewrites the file rather than appending plain bytes. Without it the append-only slab path concatenated the compressed twin's bytes onto the cached plain prefix and stamped it complete; a stopped thread never changes again, so the corrupt transcript was served forever. The locate pipeline is `find … | sort | head -1` so the pick is deterministic and prefers the plain twin. **AND THE ALREADY-CORRUPTED SLOTS HEAL THEMSELVES (review follow-up, same batch):** every slot in the field carries a PRE-provenance meta, and reading “no remotePath” as “same file” is vacuously true — the hybrid a stopped thread’s slot already held kept passing the short-circuit forever. So `sameRemote` is strict (`meta.remotePath === remotePath`), a meta without provenance is NOT valid (refetch whole ONCE, rewrite it, never delta onto it), and the cache FILE is checked independently of its meta: head magic must agree with the resolved remote, and a plain cache whose last 4KB carry a NUL byte or a zstd frame header is spliced (an append lands foreign bytes at the TAIL). Single exception: a remote already past `maxBytes` cannot be refetched whole at all (the delta path is how the slot grew there), so a byte-verified cache adopts the provenance instead of failing “too large”. **THE ADOPTION IS THE ONE DECISION THAT OUTLIVES THE TAIL WINDOW (B-7638):** the pre-fix delta path kept APPENDING after it spliced, so on a long-lived slot the marker sits far above the last 4 KB and a tail-only read called the hybrid verified. A cache slot therefore scans the WHOLE file (1 MiB chunks, 3-byte carry so a magic split across a boundary is still seen) before its bytes are trusted — gated on a meta SCHEMA MARKER (`v: 2`, written by every meta writer here), NOT on “no remotePath”: the shipped tail-only adoption stamped provenance onto the very hybrids it adopted, so `sameRemote` is true for exactly that corruption (round 2). The scan is paid ONCE per slot because the verification is WRITTEN BACK (`stampVerified`: remotePath + compressed + `v` + an `adopted` marker when the bytes were verified rather than fetched) on BOTH early-return rungs; a refused slot is left unstamped, and the “too large” error says the cache could not be verified AND that the remote is past the cap (the suffix is only reachable there, so the earlier “delete it to re-sync” was advice that could not work). **The legacy ssh rung also grows now** (round 2): stamping fixes only the repeated scan, while the harm — an over-cap slot hard-failing “too large” on its next byte — was a TWIN GAP against the slab rung's 2.187.0 delta; it now runs the same append-only delta via `tail -c +N` (1-based on GNU and BSD), same legality test, short read throws, a read that OVERTAKES the stat keeps the extra append-only bytes and stamps the real size. And a transcript SHORTER than the 4-byte magic is verifiable after all: it cannot BE a zstd frame nor hide a splice, so an empty/one-record transcript short-circuits on its cache instead of being fully re-pulled on every poll forever (a cache whose head is not a record, or a sub-magic cache under a COMPRESSED remote, is still refused). Pins: test-codex-zst ⑥/⑥b/⑥c (stub device switching remote files under one slot; a pre-written hybrid + old-shape meta healing with the remote standing still, negative-controlled against the pre-fix predicate)). **ROUND 3 — the round-2 delta's own three residuals:** ① the compression-legality clause (`!isZstPath(remotePath) && !cacheIsCompressed()`) had NO negative control on either rung — deleting it left the suite green, while the case it exists for (a host RE-compressing a finished rollout: same path, magic-verified .zst cache, cached archive shorter than the remote — every other precondition satisfied) would weld a foreign frame tail onto the old frames and serve the OLD transcript with the growth silently gone; both rungs now carry a both-compressed growth leg that dies when the clause is removed from its own copy. ② The round-2 ssh delta REPLACED the whole `cat` on the LAST rung, so a failing `tail` (remote rotated between stat and read; a host whose `tail` has no `-c +N`) hard-failed a fetch the pre-delta code completed — a delta failure now falls back to the whole `cat` when `size <= maxBytes` (failure logged VERBATIM) and stays a hard error only over the cap, where a whole re-pull is impossible by construction (so the fallback is never a cap bypass). ③ Both meta writers built a FRESH object, so the next delta erased `adopted`/`slab` — the durable provenance ① depends on, on the one slot class that can never re-earn it. ONE shared `nextMeta(fields, {whole})` spreads the prior meta on both rungs; only a WHOLE refetch clears those markers (they describe bytes no longer in the slot). Pins: test-codex-zst ⑥d/⑥e. **ROUND 4 — ONE WRITER PER SLOT:** both rungs compute the append offset from a stat taken BEFORE the remote read, so two overlapping fetches of one slot (poll + a user opening the window, two clients, goal-sync + an attach) both appended the same tail and the cache grew a DUPLICATED region — self-healing until the remote passes the doubled size, after which the next delta stamps the spliced file COMPLETE and a stopped thread serves duplicated + missing records forever (duplicated JSON trips neither byte marker). `_fetchRemoteByFind` is now a single-flight wrapper over the core `_fetchRemoteByFindOnce` (in-flight promise per cache path — the second caller awaits the first's verdict; caps come from one descriptor so coalescing cannot lose a cap), and every delta goes through `_appendDeltaAt(cachePath, offset, buf)`: open `r+`, re-read the size through that fd, write POSITIONALLY at `offset`, `false` when the slot has moved ⇒ whole refetch under the cap / loud failure over it, never a splice. Pins: test-codex-zst ⑥f (both rungs, pre-fix repro per leg). **ROUND 5 — A MOVED SLOT IS TERMINAL ON EVERY RUNG:** round 4's over-cap refusal was thrown INSIDE the data-plane `try`, whose catch degrades every failure to the ssh rung — so on a dial host with a reachable ssh fallback the refusal was swallowed silently and the ssh rung recomputed its offset from the MOVED file and spliced: right-size / wrong-bytes cache, meta stamped COMPLETE, served forever (reproduced with a foreign 203-byte append during `fsReadRange`). Three legs, each mutation-tested on its own. ① The verdict is TYPED (`slotMovedError`, code `ESLOTMOVED`) and the catch re-throws it through `_isTerminalFetchError` — a statement about the CACHE is true on every transport, only TRANSPORT failures may degrade. ② What a rung learned about the slot outlives it: `observed.moved` (read via `_slotMovedEarlier`) denies the ssh rung a delta even when the slab rung then failed for an unrelated reason (its own whole refetch dying). ③ The durable half, because the movement is invisible one poll later — the foreign bytes are simply IN the file, so `_appendDeltaAt`'s re-read offset MATCHES them and the append lands right behind them: `_prefixIsOurs(localSize, meta)` lets a delta extend only bytes this cache's own writers stamped (file ≤ `meta.size`; a SHORTER file is deliberately still growable — a positional append only writes at the end, so it is a genuine prefix after a crash or a truncation, and refusing it would strand every over-cap slot that ever crashed mid-write). Over the cap all of it is a loud failure that leaves cache+meta byte-identical, and the cap error names WHICH fault (spliced bytes vs "holds N bytes where the last fetch stamped M"). Two consequences: the whole `cat` now stamps `buf.length`, not the stat it was promised (a live transcript hands back more bytes than the probe said — the tail branch has always stamped the real length, and an under-claiming meta would make the invariant read our own fetch as foreign), and the data-plane catch LOGS every fault it swallows VERBATIM (it was silent — the 2.340.2 lost-binding class hides in exactly such a catch). Pins: test-codex-zst ⑥g (the verifier's dial+ssh scenario refused on both rungs and again on the next poll; leg isolation per guard; the pre-fix repro with all three neutered reproducing the sealed corrupt slot; the degrade log verbatim with a healthy-fetch negative control; the overtaking `cat` stamp with a pre-fix-meta control). **ROUND 6 — THE ONE-TIME OVER-STAMP HEAL (and the log that repeated itself):** round 5's "grow only what we stamped" also condemns an INNOCENT shape wearing the same signature — the pre-round-5 whole `cat` stamped the PROBE's stat while `cat` returned everything the live transcript had grown to since, so `meta.size` was SHORT on a perfectly healthy fetch. Under the cap that costs one whole re-pull; OVER it there is no whole re-pull, so every such slot (a remote stopped thread that opened yesterday) became a PERMANENT hard failure. No local scan can separate the two shapes — the round-5 corruption appends ordinary text — so the disputed bytes are checked against the source of truth: when a slot is over the cap AND its meta predates the `sizeExact` marker AND the file is longer than that meta claims, the gap `[stamp, file)` is read back (BOUNDED: `fsReadRange` on the slab rung, `tail -c +N | head -c LEN` on the ssh one) and compared byte-for-byte with the cache. Equal ⇒ genuine prefix ⇒ `meta.size = file size` + `sizeExact` + `healedStampAt`, once, and the delta rides again; not equal ⇒ round 5's refusal stands. `_overStampedLegacySlot(localSize, meta)` is the precondition (neuterable like its siblings), `sizeExact: true` is stamped by `nextMeta` and by `stampVerified` (whose early-return now also requires it, so the marker-less population shrinks by one slot per poll), and four bounds keep the heal from becoming a way around round 5: over the cap only, marker-less metas only, never on a slot `_slotMovedEarlier` says moved in this window, and the free local whole-file splice scan first (skipped when this poll's `cacheUsable` already paid for it). The re-stamp is written the moment the remote CONFIRMS the bytes — not on the fetch's own meta write, or a delta dying on the wire would throw the proof away and re-probe every poll on exactly the flaky over-cap slots. A REFUSAL, by contrast, is memoized in memory only (`_healRefusedAt`, keyed by cache path AND the size it was made on, 10 min, carrying the verdict) — stamping a slot we would not serve freezes the corruption in. Four verdicts ⇒ four different sentences appended to the cap error (`foreign` = checked mismatch, `spliced` = local marker, `moved`, `unverified` = retryable), because claiming a check that was skipped is "an error string is not a diagnosis" with the sign flipped. Second half: round 5's data-plane degrade line is rate-limited per HOST via `_warnDegradeOnce(id, msg, nowMs)` (≤1/60s, next line carries `(+N similar suppressed in the last minute)`; the heal's own probe-failure line shares that budget) — the fault it degrades on is usually persistent and every attach/poll/goal-sync tick comes through there. Pins: test-codex-zst ⑥h (pre-fix permanent failure reproduced first; heal + delta on both rungs; durability across a dead delta; a dirty same-length cache refused and memoized; a buried marker refused with no remote read; under-cap = whole refetch; a marked meta refused without asking; a probe dying on the wire = retryable; the log rate limit with a second host and a window-expiry leg — ten mutations each red on their own). **ROUND 7 — THE HEAL'S OWN COSTS, AND A COMPARISON THAT NEVER RE-ASKED:** ① the whole-file splice scan was "paid once per slot" only INSIDE one rung — `cacheUsable` runs on the slab rung and again on the ssh rung after the degradable "too large", and the slots that owe the scan are exactly the ones that REFUSE (a refused poll leaves the meta byte-identical by design, so nothing ever retires the legacy marker) ⇒ a 64 MB slot read whole, twice, on every session poll / attach / goal-sync tick, forever.
