the `--settings` flag layer only exists when the caller knows the session was spawned with one, and an unknown HOME DROPS the user layer instead of inventing `/.claude/settings.json`. **codex KEYS `origins` BY LEAF PATH FOR A TABLE-VALUED KEY (round 4, MEASURED against a real 0.153.4: `codex app-server` under an empty HOME, initialize→initialized→config/read{includeLayers:true}).** With a `[sandbox_workspace_write]` table in config.toml the origin keys are `sandbox_workspace_write.writable_roots.0` / `.network_access` / `.exclude_tmpdir_env_var` and `'sandbox_workspace_write' in origins` is **false**; a session `-c sandbox_workspace_write.network_access=true` (the exact form src/adapters/codex.js spawns with, and the form any user `codex.extraArgs` takes) lands on that LEAF as `sessionFlags`. Asking only the top level therefore filed the user's OWN config under a fabricated "packaged defaults" layer noted *"not set in any layer — the packaged default"* — the exact opposite of what the view exists to say — and left the `sessionFlags` layer, the stated reason the codex SESSION rung exists at all, EMPTY. So: a key with no top-level origin is resolved from its LEAVES — every leaf on one layer ⇒ the whole key belongs to that layer with no note; leaves SPLIT across layers ⇒ **one rule per leaf under the layer that won it** (codex's own model, the same shape `projects.<cwd>.trust_level` already used), with an array's per-index leaves collapsed to their parent path when they agree (a real config with 700 `writable_roots` produced 701 leaf origins). Only a key with NEITHER a top-level NOR a leaf origin is "the packaged default" — and that bucket never FORGES codex's `packagedDefaults` variant, whose 0.153.4 schema REQUIRES a `file` and which 0.153.4 does not list at all: when codex names that layer we use its record and its file, otherwise we say `codex built-in defaults` in our own words. A layer with `file:null` may carry a `fileNote` so the renderer stops claiming "not stored on disk" (true of `sessionFlags`, false of a bucket we synthesised). **AND "WE DROPPED THE ORIGIN MAP" IS A THIRD FACT** — `resp.originsDropped` (set by the wrapper's byte-cap ladder) files every rule under an explicit `unknown source` layer with `CODEX_CAPPED_NOTE` = *"origin unknown — the answer was capped"*, never `CODEX_DEFAULT_NOTE`; both notes are exported so no reader hand-writes either. **A PER-INDEX ORIGIN IS NOT A RULE (2026-09-07 residual).** codex keys `origins` per ARRAY INDEX and KEEPS the lower layer's indices after a higher layer REPLACED the array with a SHORTER one, so `writable_roots.1` can carry an origin while the RESOLVED config has one element. This view answers ONE question — "where does this rule come from" — and there is no rule at that index, so the leaf is DROPPED before anything is rendered: the old code printed a row with an empty value and the note "value not carried in the answer", which reads as *we could not read it* about a rule that does not exist. Dropping them BEFORE the layer-agreement test is the other half: with the phantoms in, a shorter array wholly owned by ONE layer looked SPLIT and was rendered element by element. When NO per-element origin maps onto the value in force, the key is attributed to the layer that set it with `CODEX_STALE_INDEX_NOTE` — never `defaultsBucket` ("nobody set it") and never `unknownBucket` (whose note is about the capped answer): two different facts must never share a sentence.
**src/local-oracles.js (PURE)** — ruling 6's registry, deliberately adversarial to itself: `ORACLES` (each with the argv, whether the CLI offers a JSON flag, and a PROOF = tool + date + CLI version + per-run INET connect counts) and `NOT_ORACLES` (**measured and REJECTED**, kept forever as negative controls with their counts and a verdict). See kb-design-lessons §9 for the measurements. Callers never build argv — `oracle(id)` selects a frozen entry. A NOT_ORACLES row may also carry `blocks:'<backend>.<capsPath>'`, meaning "this measurement is WHY that capability is off" (round 2, after a connecting `codex app-server` rung shipped past a table that rejects `codex doctor` for the same thing): `blockedCapability()` gives the server the record for its typed refusal and `blockingRejectionsFor()` gives the menu a disabled row shown **always** — the "only when a harness has no oracles" rule would have hidden precisely the rejection that explains a MISSING BUTTON, since codex has three shipped oracles. test-vendor-whitelist asserts the named caps row really is `false` on both tiers, so re-enabling it without a new measurement fails the build.
**src/server/permission-rules.js (ORCH, create(deps))** — the I/O + rung choice, gated on the caps row (`permissionRules`), never on a backend id. claude = the settings hierarchy off disk (1 MiB cap per file; a missing file, an unparseable one and one with no `permissions` block are THREE different notes; each `managed-settings.d/*.json` drop-in is its own source with its own path so "copy path" points at the right file). codex SESSION = the session's own wrapper via the `read-permission-rules` stdin verb — it HAS to be the session's own, because `config/read` resolves a `sessionFlags` layer (the `-c` overrides this session was spawned with) that a fresh child cannot see; codex INSTANCE = **NOT OFFERED, and that is the round-2 fix**: the first cut answered it with a bounded `codex app-server` child (the src/codex-thread-read.js pattern), which was then measured on that very code path — `strace -f -qq -e trace=network`, `env -i HOME=<empty dir>` ⇒ logged out, codex 0.153.4 — opening **7 INET connects, 2 of them :443 to chatgpt.com**, i.e. phoning the vendor before reading a local TOML, from a menu whose sibling rows advertise "no network requests (measured)". So `permissionRules.instance` is `false` for codex, `read()` answers the dedicated code `would-connect` carrying the measurement, and the proof lives permanently in src/local-oracles.js as `codex-app-server-config-read` with `blocks:'codex.permissionRules.instance'`. **THE ONLY `spawn` LEFT IN THIS FILE is the oracle runner's**, and test-vendor-whitelist pins that count — a future child has to arrive through the measured registry, which cannot accept an entry without a proof. opencode = the serve's v1 `/config`. A REMOTE session is answered honestly (`remote-session`) rather than with this machine's files, and the host guard sits ABOVE the rung choice deliberately: for a live remote codex session the frame WOULD reach the wrapper's stdin, but `wrapperCaps()` reads the sidecar the wrapper writes on ITS OWN machine, so the advert gate could only ever answer the misleading `wrapper-old` ("still starting up? try again in a moment", forever) — one honest refusal beats one with an actionable-looking lie; making it work needs a remote advert channel and is a separate change. TWO capability gates on the session rung, the 2.361.1/2.364.1 pair: the harness row says this KIND of agent answers, `wrapperCaps().permissionRules` says THIS process does — an older wrapper is refused with its start time and "Terminate + Resume", never handed a frame it drops silently. **The wrapper's answer is TRIMMED and its 32 KiB ladder now SAYS WHAT IT LOST (round 4)**: it forwards the permission keys' own origins AND their LEAF origins (head-matched, so `projects.*` and every non-permission key stay out exactly as before); over the cap it drops `origins` and sets **`originsDropped:true`** — the old ladder dropped the map and kept `ok:true`, so every key inherited "not set in any layer — the packaged default" from a map it had just deleted, and the footer only said "the list was capped"; still over the cap after the drop it answers `ok:false, reason:'read-failed'` with the byte count instead of emitting the oversized line (MEASURED against a real 0.153.4: 700 `writable_roots` = 186780 bytes full, **33719 after the drop**, i.e. the cap was decorative). `shapeWrapperAnswer` forwards `originsDropped` into `codexRulesRecord` — a WIRING PIN drives that through the real `readViaSession` seam and measures the LAYER the rules land in (the 2.355.0 unstaged-wiring law). Every refusal carries a code + `scope:'action'`. The oracle runner spawns ONLY registry argv under `agentEnv()` + the account's isolated config dir, on a POST (a GET would be pre-fetchable — "never on a timer" must not lose by accident), with both streams captured (`codex login status` answers on stderr) and a 256 KiB cap. `resolveOracleCmd(backend, refs)` is PURE and exported so **'no-runner' (no command wired for that harness) stays a different answer from 'not-installed'** — reporting the second for the first sends the reader off to install something already there. Routes: `GET /api/permission-rules`, `POST /api/local-oracle/:id` — and NO write route, ever (codex's `config/value/write`/`config/batchWrite` optimistic concurrency turns one careless write into data loss, design §4.5; the wrapper never constructs them and the suite pins that).
**src/lib/permission-rules-view.js (CLIENT)** — `loadInto`/`renderInto`/`openPermissionRulesDialog`/`runLocalOracle`/`hasRuleSurface`. HUMAN-TRIGGERED everywhere: Session Properties draws a "Show rules…" button (a panel that re-fetched on every broadcast would re-ask the session's agent on every broadcast — the codex rung is a full round trip to that session's own app-server, 20s ceiling; the codex INSTANCE rung that used to spawn a child is gone, so "a process per repaint" is no longer the reason and the comment says the true one), Manage Agents offers "Permission rules…" + one row per oracle through the shared `_rulesAndChecksItems(backend, {accountId, accountName, selectedHost})` (local machine only — a remote host's rules and CLI live on that machine). A harness with NO oracles shows its measured-and-REJECTED candidates DISABLED with the reason, because "nothing here" and "we measured these and they phone home" are different facts; a rejection carrying `blocks` is shown even when the harness DOES have oracles, because it explains a missing button rather than an empty menu. A transport failure is turned into the SAME typed record shape the server produces, so the renderer has one input and the honest-empty-state rule holds on every path. **HUMAN-TRIGGERED DOES NOT MEAN LOSE-ON-REPAINT (round 3, reproduced at 375×667):** Session Properties' `render()` opens with `root.innerHTML=''` and re-runs on every 'active-sessions' broadcast — which fires on every session create/exit/attach AND on every agent TodoWrite (coalesced to 500ms server-side), i.e. continuously while the very session you opened Properties for is working, so the loaded tree vanished within a second and the button went back to "Show rules…" (on codex that threw away a 20s agent round trip). The window now HOLDS the record (`winInfo._permRulesLoaded = {key, record}`) and re-RENDERS it after the section is rebuilt — never re-fetches, so the click stays the only thing that ever asks the agent — and the key is the QUERY it answered (backend/scope/sessionId/cwd/host), so a tree is DROPPED rather than relabelled when the question changes underneath. A broadcast landing mid-read detaches the tree and `loadInto` correctly refuses to paint a detached node, so the click handler repaints from the held record instead of holding an answer nobody sees; `loadInto` therefore returns the record on EVERY path including that one. ≤768px (measured at 375×667 in the suite): the layer head wraps, the count chip drops under the name, the copy-path button is a full-width tap target ≥20px, nothing overflows horizontally, and the oracle `<pre>` wraps instead of scrolling the page sideways.
## src/usage-origin-backfill.js (2026-09-10 — naming the history)

Run by migration `2026-09-usage-origin-backfill`. From this release the walk stamps `origin`/`wf`/`agent` and attributes an agent event to the parent project (src/usage-walker.js); every row written before it says nothing, and the ledger is permanent, so the Usage window's new cut would describe only the days since the upgrade. The migration walks the transcript tree ONCE into `rid → {origin, wf, agent, own cwd, parent cwd}` and looks up every ledger row:

- found in a MAIN transcript ⇒ `'main'`, nothing else changes;
- found in an AGENT transcript ⇒ origin/wf/agent stamped, `cwd` rewritten to the parent project's, the agent's own directory kept as `wcwd` when it differs;
- `be:'codex'` ⇒ `'main'` with NO lookup (the rule the walker states — a rollout is never a second kind of file), which also skips half the ledger's rows;
- anything else ⇒ **`'unknown'`, honestly**. Guessing `'main'` would quietly make the agent split under-report exactly where it matters.

A rid present in BOTH a main and an agent transcript (a sidechain record written to both) is `'main'` — that is the file the conversation owns, and the two carry the same project cwd anyway. It asks the walker's own `makeProjectCwdReader`, not a copy: a migration that resolved the project differently from the walk would make its rows and the walk's rows disagree about the same conversation.

Contract (the migration-runner's): every shard is COPIED VERBATIM under `data/archive/usage-origin-backfill-<day>/` (with a `_migration.json` naming who copied it) before it is rewritten atomically; a row that already carries an `origin` is left exactly as it is, so a second run — or a run after the new walk already re-scanned some files — changes nothing; an unparseable line and a non-object line are kept verbatim (we only rewrite what we can NAME); no ledger row is ever removed. Deliberately **no per-row `repairedBy` stamp** (the anchors repair's pattern): that is ~30 bytes on every one of this instance's ~500,000 rows for a fact the ledger, the archive copy and the printed report already state — and a rewritten `cwd` keeps its original in `wcwd`, so nothing it touches is unrecoverable. Deliberately **no serverNotice**: no usage moved between accounts and nothing was archived away; the ledger gained a label.

MEASURED on a COPY of this instance's stores (2026-09-10): 12 shards / **506,107 rows in → 506,107 out**, 0 unparseable, origins **main 360,707 · workflow 78,053 · subagent 14,270 · unknown 53,077** (of the unknown: 27,837 remote-host rows whose transcripts live on another machine — those carry their own origin from the next harvest, since the shipped scanner stamps it — and 25,240 local rows whose transcripts have been rotated away, 2026-01 → 2026-09); 34,587 rows re-attributed from an agent's own directory to the parent project (31,580 of them out of a worktree); 8,706 transcripts / 3.88 GB walked; 184,580 rids mapped; **31.8 s**, second run 0 changed / 0 shards rewritten. Cost stated plainly: a one-shot ~30 s boot pause on an instance with 4 GB of transcripts, printed as a report line.

## src/fixture-guard.js + src/fixture-ledger-purge.js + scripts/test-fixture-isolation.mjs (2026-09-09 — a test fixture that a production reader can see is production data)

**src/fixture-guard.js (PURE, imports nothing).** THE ONE DECLARATION of what a test fixture looks like, so no production reader can count one. Two facts and nothing else: `FIXTURE_CWD_PREFIX = 'vs-'` (the basename prefix `scripts/scratch.mjs` mints every throwaway path from, under `TMP_ROOTS`) and `FIXTURE_SID_PREFIX = 'e2e00000-0000-4000-8000-'` (the synthetic conversation-id family). Predicates: `isFixtureProjectDir(name)` (over the `cwdToProjectDir` encoding — restated here, because session-store requires THIS module and a PURE module imports nothing), `isFixtureSid`, `isFixtureCwd`, `realHomeFixtureReason`, and `fixtureLitter(entries, {now, staleMs, graceMs})` = the standing sweep as a pure decision over a directory listing, so the negative control can plant one under a throwaway home and prove the rule can go red. `REAL_HOME_FIXTURE_PREFIXES` is the ONE declared exception (`vs-wire-probe-`: it measures the INSTALLED CLI with the machine's real credentials, so a throwaway HOME would measure a different install) and `FIXTURE_STALE_MS` is shared with that probe's own sweep — two hand-written copies of one threshold is how the sweep and the probe would come to disagree about the same directory. `SWEEP_RULE` is the sentence the suite PRINTS: a rule that lives only in an assert message teaches nobody what to do when it is red.

**PURE on purpose**: three tiers ask it (the SHARED walk, SHARED discovery, the ESM test scripts) and `data/bin/vibespace-usage-scan` carries a VERBATIM INLINE COPY of the two predicates — a checkout-less ssh host cannot require `src/`, and a rule with an import is a rule that cannot be mirrored. `scripts/test-usage-walk-parity.mjs` extracts that copy from the scanner's own source, evaluates it, and drives BOTH spellings over one table (11 project-dir names × 6 session ids, asserted non-vacuous in both directions) plus one fixture tree where only the real conversation walks.

**Consumers.** `src/usage-walker.js` skips a fixture project dir and a fixture sid (claude transcripts, subagent/workflow transcripts and codex rollouts alike); `src/session-store.js` `discoverClaudeSessions` skips the same, on BOTH branches — the local readdir and the DEVICE snapshot — because the fact is about the directory, not about which transport read it. **THE COST IS STATED IN THE SOURCE:** the whole convention is skipped, so the handful of REAL turns the CI probes run in a throwaway cwd stop being ledgered (245 rows / 0.04 % of this instance's ledger), against 79,533 fabricated rows that stop being possible and a cursor file that stops growing.

**src/fixture-ledger-purge.js** (unclassified, beside `src/reading-repair.js` — a data repair, not a fact about a machine). `purgeFixtureLedger({dataDir, id})` archives every fixture row to `data/archive/fixture-ledger-rows-<date>.ndjson` WITH a per-class reason (fabricated vs a real turn in a fixture cwd — the report counts and TOKENS are per class so the fabricated half cannot hide inside the real one), rewrites each shard atomically, drops the dead `_cursors.json` entries and the synthetic `attribution.ndjson` entries, VOIDS the `costSince` of every anchor whose `(prevFetchedAt, fetchedAt]` interval contained a removed row (binary search over the sorted removed instants; the anchor RECORD is never removed — the reading is real, only the cost measured beside it is not), and archives+drops `rates.json`. An unparseable ledger line is NEVER removed: we only drop what we can NAME. Run by migration `2026-09-purge-test-fixture-ledger`; idempotent both by the ledger and by itself.

**scripts/test-fixture-isolation.mjs** (FAST tier, LAST row — within the fast tier it really does run after every suite that could litter; the heavy tier is detached, so a heavy-tier leak is caught by the NEXT push's fast tier, and the header says so). It reads the real `~/.claude/projects` and nothing else, and carries three grep-derived censuses that PRINT what they walked: (a) no suite WRITES under the real `~/.claude` — reading it is fine, and both directions have synthetic controls; (b) every suite that spawns `server.js` AND writes a transcript NAMES a `HOME` in that spawn env — the defect itself, as a property of the source; (c) the suites carrying a synthetic sid mint it via `fixtureSid()`, clean up on signals, and census the real home themselves. Its strongest control is the RETIRED BYTES: `git show master:scripts/test-chat-paging.mjs` through `scripts/git-env.mjs`'s sanitized environment, asserting the census catches both offenders exactly as they shipped; a tree git cannot read is a LOUD SKIP. It exempts itself from (a) and (b) because its controls spell the forbidden shapes inline — and PAYS for both exemptions (its real-home section contains no write call; every child it starts is `git`) while asserting each exemption is still LIVE.

**THE STANDING SWEEP GIVES AN UNDECLARED FIXTURE DIR THE SAME IN-FLIGHT FLOOR EVERY SWEEPER ALREADY HAS (r3, 2026-09-09).** `fixtureLitter` tolerated age only for a DECLARED prefix, so a fixture dir a CONCURRENT checkout (this box hosts ~160) put in the real home turned the mandatory pre-push gate red in every OTHER worktree — reproduced live while running the full fast tier, on a `-tmp-vs-chat-e2e-cwd-<mkdtemp>` name only master's pre-fix `test-chat-e2e` can mint. The tree already had the answer thirty lines away: no sweeper here (the wire probe's, test-chat-e2e's) may delete a fixture dir younger than `FIXTURE_STALE_MS`, because it may be a run in flight — so the gate was demanding a removal nothing was allowed to perform, on a directory the walk and discovery both provably refuse. `graceMs` is therefore OPT-IN and passed by EXACTLY ONE caller: §4, the whole-directory sweep, at that same shared constant. The four PER-SUITE censuses pass none, and must not — they call `fixtureLitter(added)` on entries already diffed against a pre-run listing, whose mtimes are ≈ now, so a grace there would spare the suite's own litter. The branch is guarded on `graceMs > 0` because with the default `0` an entry whose mtime equals `now` has `ageMs === 0` and `0 <= 0` would relax every strict caller silently. A spared entry is NAMED with its age and `IN_FLIGHT_WHY`, carries `declared:false` (the declared spare keeps its own reason — the two answers stay distinguishable), and becomes an offender the moment it goes stale. §6 is the WIRING PIN: grep-derived over every suite, printed, asserting both halves (no other suite passes `graceMs`; §4 still does). DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: sweeping the other three families' stale residue — that turns this read-only census into a writer and breaks the §4 read-only property census (a) is paid with; the printed `rm -rf` remedy stays for genuinely stale litter.

**CENSUS (a) IS TRANSITIVE, AND ITS EXEMPTIONS ARE SCOPED (r2, 2026-09-09).** The rule has been widened TWICE and both misses were "one more hop": round 1 widened where the real HOME comes from (`os.homedir()` vs `process.env.HOME || os.homedir()`); r2 widened how the value REACHES the write. The shipped matcher required the call's first argument to BE the bound name or `path.join(<bound name>, …)`, so `const p = path.join(REAL_PROJECTS, d.name); fs.rmSync(p, {recursive:true})` in test-chat-e2e — an `rm -rf` under the developer's own home — produced `bound names ["REAL_PROJECTS"], hits []` while the suite printed a clean sheet. `realHomeWriters` therefore takes the FIXPOINT of "a name derived from a name already rooted at the real home" (the known name as the HEAD of a right-hand side — alias, `X + '/y'`, template — or anywhere inside a `path.join`/`path.resolve`), and the write matcher asks whether the FIRST ARGUMENT mentions one, bounded by `[^,)]` so it cannot cross into a later argument (a real-home path passed as CONTENT is not a write TO it). Over-inclusive on purpose, cost MEASURED over all 197 suites: exactly one new file flagged. **And the two write exemptions are paid for DIFFERENTLY, each with the property that bounds ITS damage:** test-stdout-registry PLANTS, so it pays FILE-scoped with the declared `vs-wire-probe-` prefix + a cleanup that survives a signal; test-chat-e2e DELETES only names it minted itself, so it pays REGION-scoped — `realHomeWritersOutside` re-runs the census over the file with the `// >>> real-home sweep` … `// <<< real-home sweep` block cut out and requires EMPTY (a second real-home write anywhere else in that "exempt" suite goes red), plus a pin that the block only DELETEs and only behind all three gates (`isFixtureProjectDir`, the `chat-e2e` substring, `FIXTURE_STALE_MS`). A missing sentinel is a FAILURE, never an empty region that passes vacuously. **The exemption is the dangerous half of a census** — scope it to the smallest unit the code shape allows.

### scripts/ci.mjs + scripts/git-hooks/pre-push (THE RELEASE GATE, two tiers since 2026-09-07 / B-4c5a)

**WHAT IT IS.** `scripts/ci.mjs` is the whole release gate: the tier table, both runners, the detached launcher, the push-blocking verdict, the status printer and the census self-test. It is the ONE file that decides what "the gate" means, and it is imported (never re-executed — the bottom `import.meta.url` guard) by `scripts/test-architecture.mjs` §43 so the census runs inside `npm run build`.

**WHY IT WAS SPLIT.** The single battery had grown to 85 suites / **11.5 min measured on the dev box** (test-desktop-resume-paging alone 224 s, then jobs-engine 71 s, client-boot 70 s, collab-live-counter 53 s, opencode-plugin 41 s, acp-harness 33 s…). That is longer than anyone waits before a push and longer than GitHub's SSH idle timeout — which is exactly why the 2.369.51 green-marker dance ("run the gate as a background job FIRST, then push") exists, and why `VIBESPACE_SKIP_CI=1` had started to look reasonable. **A gate people route around is not a gate.** So the battery is two tiers with two different jobs, and the honesty is in the naming: the fast tier's promise is "this push is not obviously broken", not "this release is good".

**THE TWO TIERS.** `SUITES` is a flat table of `{ name, tier, why? }`. `tier:'fast'` = build + everything under ~10 s that does not launch a browser → **73 suites, 86–105 s wall measured on the dev box** (build ~1.9 s + 73 suites; 86/89/91 s before round 2, 94/98 s after, **101–105 s after round 3** (both real haiku turns, one on a clean tree with the green marker written) — the launcher self-test grew 5.5 s → 11.6 s when it took on the concurrency legs, → 16.2 s when it took on the supersede A/B *and* the retry control that keeps that guard from swallowing the flaky path, → 23.8 s once round 5 added the REAL `fastGate` A/B (isolated / in place / neutered), and → **28.3 s** at round 6 (five more REAL `fastGate` arms for the absent-suite rule plus two real heavy runs), which is the price of a guard having controls that die with it; round 5 measured **build 1.8 s + 72 suites in 106.8 s = 108.5 s** on this box, with the 73rd (`test-chat-e2e`) RED for a vendor `api_error` on the CI subscription — reproduced identically on the untouched base commit, i.e. a credential/quota fact about the box, not about the tier; `npm run ci`, fail-fast, the pre-push gate, writes `.git/ci-green` on a clean tree exactly as before). `tier:'heavy'` = **97 suites, ~16.2-16.5 min measured (971 s, 980 s and 992 s over three full runs; the 971 s one is round 2's, through `npm run ci:heavy` in its own worktree at the commit, 97 suites, zero flaky)** (`npm run ci:heavy`), and EVERY heavy row states what makes it heavy — `chrome` (**the fast tier never launches a browser**: a browser leg's wall time follows machine load, and a pre-push gate has to be predictable), `server` (boots a real worktree server), `cli` (drives a real agent CLI/app-server), `binary` (needs the real opencode binary), `slow` (>10 s of real processes) or `adopted` (see below) — with its measured wall time, because "heavy" without a reason is where suites go to be forgotten. **THE ONE DELIBERATE EXCEPTION IS `test-chat-e2e`**: ~10 s and it boots a server AND spends real quota, so by the rule it is heavy — it stays FAST by owner decision, because one real haiku turn is the only proof in the whole battery that a real turn works, and a gate that cannot answer "does chat still work" is not worth two minutes.

**THE CENSUS (the item this work was filed as).** Before the split, **99 of the 184 files matching `scripts/test-*.mjs` were in no list at all** — they neither ran nor were written down as skipped, so nobody could tell "deliberately not gated" from "forgotten" (test-usage-estimator and test-task-wakeup-card each spent months in that hole and joined the gate only after an incident said so). Now every one of them is in exactly one tier or in `EXCLUDED` **with a reason**, asserted by `--census` and by test-architecture §43 (which also carries a NEGATIVE CONTROL — an unclassified name, a ghost entry and a duplicate must all be reported, because a census that cannot go red is not a census). The census reads **readdir, not `git ls-files`** — the opposite of §42 round 5, and deliberately: §42 reads the index because the PRODUCT writes runtime products into the working tree (the 64 MB `data/bin/rclone`), while nothing writes `scripts/test-*.mjs`, and the case this census exists for is precisely the suite you just wrote and have not committed yet. Reading the index would let exactly that one fall through.

**WHAT `EXCLUDED` MAY SAY.** It is the escape hatch and it is deliberately uncomfortable to add to: an entry there is a suite nobody runs, and every reason carries the measurement that produced it. The four categories in use (16 entries): (a) *needs an argument or a real remote machine* — `test-agentd-real-ssh <hostId>`, `test-host-mounts <hostId>`; (b) *red right now*, quoted assert by assert so it is a debt with evidence rather than a shrug — test-agents-overview, test-sys-panel, test-window-menu, test-agentd-m3m4, test-auto-graduate, test-integration-toggle, every one of them a suite that had been in NO runner and rotted unseen; (c) *not runnable more than once, or not on a shared machine* — test-desktop-reorder passes on a clean run and fails on the immediately following one (pass/fail/pass/fail over four consecutive runs: fixed CDP port, no `--user-data-dir`, so run N+1 inherits run N), test-stage-preview hard-codes PORT=3987 and failed 3/3 while an orphaned server from another checkout held it; (d) *already chained by `npm run build`* — architecture, ws-contract, session-schema, bundle-globals.

**THE COST OF LETTING THE FAST TIER OVERLAP THE HEAVY ONE (measured, round 2, deliberately not "fixed").** The launcher self-test drives its OWN machine lock so a push never waits sixteen minutes for somebody else's heavy run — which means a fast tier (and any gate tooling) can run WHILE the heavy tier runs. On a loaded box that overlap is not free: running a 12-case mutation battery alongside a heavy run turned `test-incident` (4 s normally) into a 13.8 s failure and then a 37.3 s one, and `test-queue-steer` into two failures — both at browser interaction, both passing in isolation immediately afterwards at 6.1 s and 9.3 s. The tier went RED for a commit that was fine, and retry-once did not rescue it because the load outlasted both attempts. The trade is still right (making the fast tier queue behind the heavy tier would be worse), and the answer is NOT to soften what counts as red — that is the laundering the split explicitly refuses. It is: don't run the gate's own tooling next to a heavy run, and when a red's failures are all browser-interaction timeouts, re-run before believing it. Written down because the next person to see this will otherwise re-diagnose it.

**THE TIER IS RETRIED ONCE BEFORE IT IS CALLED RED.** This verdict blocks a push, and a large part of the adopted set hard-codes a port or a `/tmp` path — on a box hosting several checkouts, another one squatting `:3987` is not a regression in the code being pushed. So a failing heavy suite is run a second time; if it passes it is recorded as `flaky` in the marker (and printed by `ci:status` and the Diagnostics row) instead of red. **Flaky is not laundered into green**: it does not block, but the marker, the log and both surfaces say the suite failed once. A suite that fails twice is red.

**THE HEAVY RUN IS DETACHED, AND IT RUNS THE SHA IT NAMES.** After the fast tier is green the hook calls `ci.mjs --heavy-launch <sha>`, which spawns `--heavy --sha=<sha> --isolate` with `detached:true` + `unref()` (no setsid/nohup dependency; the project's own detached-job primitive — jobs.js / data/bin/job-wrapper.js — needs a running server and a session token, so it is not reachable from a git hook) writing to `data/ci-heavy/<sha>.log` with `<sha>.pid` beside it. Two details are load-bearing: **(1) the child gets a SANITIZED git environment** (`scripts/git-env.mjs`, the one spelling shared with test-architecture §42 — a pre-push hook exports `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_INDEX_FILE`/`GIT_PREFIX`, and every heavy suite runs `git worktree add`; the class that once REINITIALISED the production checkout). **(2) `--isolate` runs the tier in a detached worktree at the pushed commit**, because the working tree keeps moving under a ten-minute run and a marker that NAMES a sha has to have tested that sha (it also keeps the #127 law: never boot server.js against the repo's PRODUCTION `data/`). **Since round 2 `npm run ci:heavy` IS `--heavy --isolate`** — it is the command a blocked push is told to run, so it must always be able to write the marker that clears the block. `--heavy` without `--isolate` still tests the working tree, but only a CLEAN one can earn a marker, so a dirty tree is REFUSED at t=0 (exit 2) unless `--dirty-ok` says "run it anyway, I know there will be no verdict".

**THE BLOCK RULE.** `--check-heavy` (the hook's FIRST step, before the two minutes of fast tier, asked ONCE PER PUSHED REF — see round 2) blocks the push when a `<sha>.red` marker names a commit that is an ANCESTOR of the commit being pushed and no green run for a DESCENDANT of it exists. Markers for commits this repository no longer knows (amended/rebased away) are ignored — they describe a history nobody is pushing. The message names the red sha, its failing suites and the log path, and says how to clear it (fix, then `npm run ci:heavy`, or the existing `VIBESPACE_SKIP_CI=1`). A checker that itself throws prints a loud warning and does NOT block — a broken meter must never become an outage — but it is never silent (§no-silent-failures). Note the shape: **the heavy tier does not delay a push, it delays the push AFTER the one it failed on**, so nothing gets stacked on a known-red commit while the feedback stays out of the developer's critical path.

**WHERE THE VERDICT SURFACES.** `npm run ci:status` prints the last runs per sha (+ any in flight, + whether HEAD is blocked); `GET /api/ci-heavy` (src/server/ops-routes.js — read-only, small local JSON files, **no git**: "is HEAD blocked" is an ancestry question and belongs to the CLI) feeds a "Release gate — heavy tier" section in the ⚙ → Diagnostics report, which is absent when there are no runs (a deployment that never pushes shows nothing new). GREEN/RED/RUNNING are printed untranslated in both surfaces — they are the gate's own vocabulary, the marker files are literally `<sha>.green` / `<sha>.red`.

**ROUND 2 — WHAT AN ADVERSARIAL READ OF THE SPLIT FOUND (2026-09-07, four defects, each reproduced first).** The split made "two gate runs at once" the DESIGN rather than the accident, and three of the four findings are consequences of that.

**① TWO HEAVY TIERS ON ONE BOX ATE EACH OTHER.** `heavyLaunch` refused only a twin for the SAME sha, so two pushes inside the ~16-minute heavy window started two full tiers. They are not independent: `test-attach-ack` bound a fixed `:3991` and checked its worktree out at a fixed `/tmp/vs-ack-smoke` **which it force-removed first**; three more suites share `:3991` and four share `:3989`. So each run deleted the other's checkout and stole its ports, and the loser wrote a RED that blocked the next push — a verdict the retry-once absorber cannot rescue, because the competing run holds the fixture for its whole duration. This box hosts **~160 worktrees of this repository** driven by parallel agents, so cross-checkout concurrency is the normal case. The fix is two mechanisms, because the resource is the MACHINE and the marker directory is per checkout: **(a) the launcher supersedes** — a run in flight for an ANCESTOR of the sha being pushed is SIGTERMed (the newer commit subsumes it and its half-finished verdict is worthless), a run for the same sha is refused as before, and anything else is launched anyway and queues, because refusing would leave that commit with no heavy coverage at all; **(b) the run takes an exclusive MACHINE lock** — `/tmp/vibespace-ci-heavy-<uid>.lock`, per uid so two users never fight over a file they cannot unlink; the path is literal `/tmp` and deliberately NOT `os.tmpdir()`, which follows TMPDIR and would therefore give two agents with different TMPDIRs one "machine lock" each while the things it protects (a bound port, the literal `/tmp` checkouts the suites claim) do not move with TMPDIR at all (os.tmpdir() stays as the fallback where `/tmp` does not exist; `machineTmpDir` is exported so the gate's own gate can prove TMPDIR does not move it) — and waits, bounded (40 min default, `--lock-wait-ms`; the queue is bounded by that budget rather than managed — a waiter is one parked node process, and supersession already collapses same-lineage pushes), before spending a build. Timing out writes **no verdict** and says so, leaving a `<sha>.skipped` note so `ci:status` and Diagnostics can state the absence rather than looking like "nobody has pushed lately". A lock whose holder is gone is STOLEN (otherwise one crash blocks the tier forever); a lock that cannot be created at all (read-only tmp) never stops the gate — the run proceeds and the marker records `unlocked`. Superseding also forced two more fixes, both found by MUTATION-TESTING the first one. **(i)** node's default SIGTERM does not run `finally`, so the heavy child installs SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP handlers that remove the worktree, its `git worktree list` registration (which `worktree prune` can NEVER remove — the directory still exists) and the lock. The first version of that leg killed the child as soon as the worktree DIRECTORY appeared, and passed with the handlers deleted — because **git cleans up its own interrupted `worktree add`**, so the leg was measuring git. The fixture now waits for the node_modules symlink heavyGate makes only after the add SUCCEEDS; with the corrected timing the A/B is clean (handlers on ⇒ gone/unregistered/unlocked; off ⇒ all three left behind). **(ii)** That corrected timing then exposed a defect in the fix itself: **a signal handler cannot preempt a synchronous run.** heavyGate is `spawnSync` from top to bottom, so a SIGTERM delivered mid-build sits on the event loop until the whole tier is over — the superseded run kept going and then stamped a marker whose build had been KILLED, i.e. a RED for the very commit the newer run replaced. So the abort is also a synchronous QUESTION asked between suites, on three independent pieces of evidence: our pid file is gone (the superseding launcher removes it — and the child is TOLD it has one via `--pid-file`, because a check that armed itself on first sight could not fire when the supersede landed before its first look; the launcher writes the file BEFORE the spawn, pid 0 then rewritten, so the reverse race cannot happen either), the machine lock is no longer ours, or a child died on a signal we did not send (`killedFromOutside` — spawnSync reports ETIMEDOUT for our OWN budget kill, and a hung suite IS a red, so laundering a hang is exactly what that clause prevents). Any of them ⇒ stop, say why, write NO verdict. **(iii)** And the question has to be asked ONE MORE PLACE than the loop top: supersession SIGTERMs the process GROUP, so the suite in flight dies of our own kill and lands in RETRY-ONCE — the superseded run then re-ran a whole heavy suite (up to its budget) while still HOLDING the machine lock, with the newer run printing "waiting up to 40 min for the machine". That is the exact opposite of why supersession kills instead of queueing. Retry-once exists for a flaky FIXTURE, and its answer here is discarded anyway (this run writes no verdict), so `abandoned()` is asked again immediately before it.

**THE MUTATION HARNESS IS TRACKED (scripts/dbg-ci-mutations.mjs).** "Every guard has an assert that dies with it" is a claim, so it has evidence: 23 mutations, each removing one guard from the REAL product file and requiring the suite that holds it to go RED. It is deliberately NOT `scripts/test-*.mjs` (it edits the product and takes ~20 min, so the census must not see it) and it obeys invariant ⑳ the hard way: signal handlers are not enough — the script spends nearly all its wall time inside `spawnSync`, so a SIGTERM sits queued and a SIGKILL runs nothing — measured twice in one afternoon, once stranding the pre-push hook and once stranding `killedFromOutside = () => false` in ci.mjs, i.e. a gate with its own abort evidence disabled. The real protection is a SELF-HEAL at start, out of a SIDECAR — `TMPDIR/vs-ci-mutations-backup-<uid>.json`, the exact pre-mutation bytes, written before the first mutation and removed on a clean finish — and NOT out of `git show HEAD:<path>`, for two reasons that are the whole point: these files are usually being WORKED on (HEAD's copy would throw away the very edit the battery is being run to check), and a mutation can be a DELETION (`to: ''`), which leaves no replacement text to recognise. With the sidecar the test is EXACT rather than heuristic: a file is healed only when it is byte-equal to the backup with one of the mutations applied to it, which nothing but our own stranded damage can look like. **PID IDENTITY, TWO THRESHOLDS:** pid records and the lock carry `cmd`, a fragment of the child's own argv checked against `/proc`, so a recycled pid can neither block every future launch nor make a lock unstealable; a record that does not say is trusted as before, because for a READ (refuse a launch, wait for a lock) unknown is not wrong. **Superseding is a KILL** — of a process GROUP — so it demands positive evidence instead: `looksLikeHeavyRun(pid)` asks `/proc` whether that pid is running `ci.mjs --heavy` and answers NO when it cannot tell, and a run it will not identify is left alone to queue on the lock (slower, never destructive). That is the cli-identity rule in miniature: identify a process by what it IS running, and never let a pid file's say-so authorise a signal. Measured on the production path (two `--heavy-launch` ~20 ms apart, default lock): the second prints `another heavy run holds … — waiting`, then runs, and both get honest greens; with the second commit descending from the first, the older run is superseded and leaves NO marker.

**② `npm run ci:heavy` DECIDED AT t=0 THAT IT WOULD WRITE NOTHING, AND SAID SO AT t=16 min — UNDER A LINE THAT SAID GREEN.** The dirty-tree refusal was evaluated before the build and printed after the whole run, and the summary still said `HEAVY GATE GREEN`. So the one command a blocked developer is told to run cost them the whole tier and left them just as blocked. Worse, the block message also offered "(or wait for the next push's background run)" — but that run is launched BY a push and the push is what is being refused: a door that only opens from the other side. Now the refusal is UP FRONT (exit 2, before the build, naming both ways forward), `npm run ci:heavy` is `--isolate` so it always earns a marker, the closing line says `NO VERDICT WRITTEN (<reason>)` whenever the marker branch was skipped, and the block message names only reachable recovery.

**③ THE VERDICT WAS ABOUT HEAD, NOT ABOUT WHAT WAS BEING PUSHED.** The hook called `--check-heavy` with no `--head` even though it had already collected every pushed sha into `PUSHED_SHAS` for the launch loop. `git push origin main` from a different branch therefore shipped a commit riding on a heavy-red ancestor with no block and no message. Now the hook asks once per pushed ref with `--head=<sha>`.

**④ A FAST-TIER SUITE CANNOT CLAIM A MACHINE-GLOBAL NAME.** `test-ci-heavy-launch` is in the FAST tier on purpose (the launcher is a silent-failure path — if detaching breaks, nothing throws and the only symptom is `ci:status` staying empty), but the slice it launched was `test-attach-ack`, so a push-blocking, fail-fast, no-retry suite depended on `:3991` and on `/tmp/vs-ack-smoke`. Measured: with a bare listener on `:3991`, that slice hangs to its budget. Three fixes: the slice is now a pure-logic heavy suite (`test-eml`) and the launcher self-test drives its OWN machine lock; `test-attach-ack` uses `freePort()` + `mkdtemp` and no longer force-removes a shared path (`test-restore-smoke`'s `3971 + pid%20` and `test-proxy-post`'s fixed pair went the same way — the split's own field notes record an orphan on `:3987` taking down three suites); and the rule is now an ASSERT — `machineGlobalFixtures` (PURE, in ci.mjs) over every fast-tier suite plus, transitively, the slice this one launches. The detector is deliberately narrow (a port DERIVED from `freePort()`/env is not a claim; a `/tmp` string that is only a fixture VALUE creates nothing) and it strips comments first, which it learned by flagging **itself**: the comment in test-ci-gate explaining "a verbatim `const PORT = 3991` control made the suite report itself" made the suite report itself. Its negative controls therefore live in `scripts/fixtures/machine-global-shapes/` — a control has to read as data. Same class, found while fixing it: the E2E's "no worktree left behind" assert compared `git worktree list` line counts and searched for ANY `vs-ci-heavy-` entry, both of which another checkout's concurrent heavy run fails for us; it now asks about the one worktree named after its own sha and pid.

**⑤ SUPERSESSION KILLED THE SUITE AND THEN SPENT A RETRY ON IT (round 3, found by RUNNING the round-2 flow end to end).** Superseding SIGTERMs the process GROUP, so the heavy suite in flight dies of *our own* kill — and retry-once then re-ran it, a whole heavy suite (up to its budget), before the loop top asked `abandoned()` again. The superseded run HELD the machine lock for that entire retry while the newer run printed `waiting up to 40 min for the machine`: the exact opposite of ①(a)'s reason for killing instead of queueing. Measured in a throwaway repository driving the REAL hook (a 90 s heavy stub, superseded 6 s in): the newer run sat waiting, the older one re-ran the corpse. The verdict was never wrong — `killedFromOutside` is sticky, so that run writes no marker either way — the COST was: supersession stopped freeing the machine, which is the only reason it exists. The fix is one ordering change (ask `abandoned()` BEFORE spending the retry, not only at the loop top) and it is verdict-identical by construction; re-measured on the same fixture, the superseding run gets the lock and finishes 3 s after the push, with `0` retries in the superseded log. **Retry-once is for a flaky FIXTURE** (another checkout squatting `:3987`), never for a failure we caused ourselves.

**THE MUTATION BATTERY IS NOW IN THE REPOSITORY: `scripts/dbg-ci-mutations.mjs`** (deliberately NOT `test-*.mjs` — it edits the product and takes minutes, and the census must never adopt it; `node scripts/dbg-ci-mutations.mjs`, `--reap-only` for just the cleanup). It is the evidence behind "every guard has an assert that dies with it" that both round-2 commits cite, and it lived in `/tmp`, so nobody else could re-run it. Round 2 recorded that it "now restores on signals too". Measured in round 3: it does not, and cannot, for the same reason heavyGate could not — **it spends ~all of its wall time inside `spawnSync`, so a SIGTERM sits queued behind the child**, and a `SIGKILL` (or the timeout that killed it once already) leaves the product file MUTATED. It happened again: a stale battery from a dead session was found still running against this worktree, and killing it stranded `killedFromOutside = () => false` in `scripts/ci.mjs`. What actually contains this is not the handler but the gate's own rules — a dirty tree earns no `.git/ci-green`, and `--heavy` refuses one at t=0 — plus a SELF-HEAL at start out of a SIDECAR (`TMPDIR/vs-ci-mutations-backup-<uid>.json`, the exact pre-mutation bytes of the three files it edits, written before the first mutation and unlinked on a clean finish): a file is restored only when it is byte-equal to `backup.replace(from, to)` for one of the mutations. `git show HEAD:<path>` was the first version and is wrong twice over — these files are usually being WORKED on, so HEAD's copy discards the very edit the battery is being run to check, and a DELETION mutation (`to: ''`) leaves no replacement text for "does it carry a mutant's text" to see. It also REAPS what it causes: several mutations exist to KILL a heavy run, and a run that dies without its `finally` leaves a full checkout in TMPDIR plus a `git worktree list` registration `worktree prune` can never remove (the directory still exists) — measured 196 MB across 18 registrations on this box after a few rounds. The scratch worktree is named `vs-ci-<tier>-<sha8>-<pid>` (round 5 gave the FAST tier one too, for a pushed ref whose tip is not HEAD), so the pid in the name is the identity: reap only that shape, only when the pid is gone, and EPERM counts as ALIVE. **And `prune` is not enough**: git takes its OWN transient lock (reason `initializing`) while it checks a new worktree out, and prune skips a locked worktree forever — so a run killed inside that window (which is what the SIGTERM mutations do) leaves a registration whose directory is gone and which nothing will ever remove; four had accumulated here. The reaper unlocks exactly that shape — our naming, dead pid, directory gone, reason literally `initializing` — because any other reason is a human saying don't touch this, with a negative control that keeps one. A tool that edits the product is subject to invariant ⑳ exactly like a suite is.

**ROUND 4 — WHAT AN ADVERSARIAL READ OF ROUNDS 2-3 FOUND (2026-09-07, four defects, each reproduced against the REAL ci.mjs / the REAL tracked hook in throwaway repositories before it was fixed — plus a fifth, ⑩, that the round's own runs produced).** Three of the four are the same shape: a check that answers a question it was never asked, and answers it in the direction that says "all is well".

**⑥ A CRASHED SUITE READ AS A SUPERSESSION — AND THE ACTIONS HEAVY JOB WENT GREEN FOR IT (high).** `killedFromOutside` was `r.signal && !(our own ETIMEDOUT)`, i.e. ANY signal but one. Measured on this box, both of the ways a suite dies of memory are signals: a **V8 heap-limit OOM** exits `{status:null, signal:'SIGABRT'}` (V8 prints `FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit` and calls `abort()` itself) and an **external-memory OOM** is taken by the kernel as `{status:null, signal:'SIGKILL'}`; a native crash is `SIGSEGV`/`SIGBUS`/`SIGILL`/`SIGFPE`. Any of those made `abandoned()` true, so the tier STOPPED at that suite, skipped every suite after it, wrote NO marker — and, because `failed` is empty for an abandoned run, `failed.length ? 1 : 0` returned **0**. The Actions heavy job's only signal IS the exit code (it runs `--heavy --dirty-ok` on a runner that is thrown away), so a tier that crashed and then ran nothing showed a **green tick**, and locally nothing blocked the next push. The fix is two lines with two different jobs: `OUTSIDE_SIGNALS = ['SIGTERM','SIGINT','SIGHUP']` — supersession sends SIGTERM (`process.kill(-pid,'SIGTERM')`), Ctrl-C sends SIGINT, a lost terminal sends SIGHUP, and that is the whole set of signals somebody SENDS this run — and `if (abandonedWhy) return 4` so an aborted tier can never exit 0. **SIGKILL is deliberately on the RED side** even though an operator's `kill -9` lands there too: the two are indistinguishable from inside the runner and the costs are not symmetrical — a wrong RED blocks one push and is cleared by re-running `npm run ci:heavy`, a wrong "abandoned" is a silent green for a tier that never ran. Exit codes are now **0 green · 1 red · 2 refused · 3 never got the machine lock · 4 ABORTED**; 0 and 1 are the only VERDICTS and no no-verdict path may exit 0. Regression: `test-ci-heavy-launch` (1f) drives a stub REPOSITORY whose first heavy slice is `process.abort()` (the same signal as the OOM, in 3 ms instead of minutes and gigabytes) and whose second is an ordinary red — the tier must write a RED marker NAMING BOTH and exit 1 — with the pre-fix module (both guards reverted) as the control: no marker, the second suite never runs, exit 0. Plus the truth table in `test-ci-gate` §6, which now reads `OUTSIDE_SIGNALS` from the module instead of re-spelling it.

**⑦ THE `.git/ci-green` SHORTCUT WAS ABOUT THE CHECKED-OUT COMMIT (high) — round 2 ③ again, in the file round 2 ③ edited.** The marker branch was keyed to HEAD + a clean tree + <60 min and never consulted `PUSHED_SHAS`, so `git push origin <other-branch>` skipped the WHOLE fast tier for a never-gated commit *and printed* `fast gate already GREEN on this exact tree` while doing it. Reproduced through the real hook with real pre-push stdin: standing on main with a fresh marker, pushing `refs/heads/feature` whose tip adds `src/broken.js` ⇒ no fast run at all. Now every pushed sha must BE the marker's sha and an empty `PUSHED_SHAS` never takes the shortcut (nothing was proven about a list we do not have). **No test drove the marker branch at all** before this round — that is how a defect round 2 had already fixed once, elsewhere, survived in the same file; `test-ci-gate` §4 now creates `.git/ci-green` in the throwaway repository and asserts the positive case, the other-branch case, a marker naming some third commit, and the pre-fix hook (that one clause deleted) as the control.

**⑧ "DOCS-ONLY" WAS INFERRED FROM AN EMPTY FILE LIST (medium).** Two different things produce one. (a) For a NEW BRANCH (remote sha = zeros) the hook inspected the TIP COMMIT only, so `[code commit][docs commit]` pushed as a new branch printed "docs-only push — gate skipped" with ZERO gate calls — **this branch's own history has exactly that shape**. A new branch publishes its whole unpublished range, so that is what is asked now: `git log --name-only --format= <sha> --not --remotes` (measured: tip-only sees `docs/nb.md`, the range sees `docs/nb.md src/nb.js`; with no remotes configured it lists everything, which is the conservative direction). (b) `git diff` / `git log` FAILING — an unresolvable range (a remote sha this checkout never fetched: `fatal: Invalid revision range`, exit 128), a broken repository — also yields an empty list, so the gate read its own inability to answer as "no code changed". The exit status is now checked and a non-zero one means NOT docs-only, **said out loud** with the command and git's own first line (§no-silent-failures). And the docs-only exit MOVED BELOW the heavy verdict: a red ancestor is red whether or not this push carries code, and a docs commit is more work stacked on a known-broken commit. Controls: the pre-fix hook for each shape (tip-only, no exit-status check, docs-only exiting first — the last one built by MOVING the block back rather than approximating it, because the guard is an ORDERING).

**⑨ DOCS THAT CONTRADICTED THE CODE'S OWN SAFETY RULES (low).** CLAUDE.md said the heavy tier "takes an exclusive lock in `os.tmpdir()`" — the exact thing invariant ⑩ exists to forbid, and a maintainer following it would reintroduce round 2 ①(b). This file said the mutation harness restores from `git show HEAD:<path>` — the first version, replaced in round 3 by the sidecar precisely because HEAD's copy discards the edit under test and a DELETION mutation leaves nothing to recognise. Both now state the implemented rule, and the fast tier's stated range carries the measurement rounds 3-4 actually produced (101/104/105 s) rather than the pre-round-3 numbers.

**⑩ THE GATE'S OWN CLEANUP ASSERT WAS A COIN TOSS UNDER LOAD (low, found by running the fast tier for this round).** `test-ci-heavy-launch` waits for the launched run's MARKER and then reads, once, whether the pid file and the isolated worktree are gone — but the marker is written inside heavyGate's `try` and `cleanup()` is its `finally`, so "the run finished" and "the run has tidied up" are two moments with a `git worktree remove --force` + `git worktree prune` between them, against a repository this box shares with ~160 checkouts. Measured: the worktree assert failed inside a full `npm run ci` and passed in isolation seconds later (62 ms of cleanup), i.e. a FALSE RED in a fast-tier, fail-fast, push-blocking suite — the exact outcome the split exists to remove. Both asserts now WAIT for the state they are asserting (bounded, 30 s) and print how long it took, so a cleanup that suddenly needs 25 s is still a finding rather than a silent pass. Invariant ⑲ said a cleanup assert must outlive the tool that cleans up FOR you; this is its other half — **it must also outlive the tool that cleans up AFTER itself, because finishing and tidying are not the same event.**

**INVARIANTS ADDED (⑳a-⑳d, numbered here because ⑰-㉒ are taken).** **⑳a A CRASH IS A VERDICT.** "Killed from outside" is an ALLOWLIST of the signals somebody SENDS a run; every other signal is a fact about the code under test. A predicate written as "any X except the one I thought of" will collect every X nobody thought of, and it will collect them on the side that says all is well. **⑳b NO NO-VERDICT PATH MAY EXIT 0.** A tier that did not finish must be distinguishable from one that passed by the ONE channel a CI runner reads. `failed.length ? 1 : 0` is not that test — `failed` is empty for a run that stopped before it could judge anything. **⑳c THE ANSWER IS ABOUT THE REFS BEING PUSHED — EVERY TIME IT IS ASKED.** Round 2 fixed this for `--check-heavy`; the marker shortcut in the same hook kept asking about HEAD for two more rounds because nothing exercised it. When a rule is corrected in one place, grep for every other consumer of the same fact in the same file — and if a branch has no test at all, that is where the correction did not land. **⑳e A CLEANUP ASSERT MUST OUTLIVE THE CLEANUP.** ⑲ said it must outlive the tool that tidies up FOR you; the other half is that "the run finished" and "the run has tidied up" are two moments — a marker written in a `try` and a cleanup in the `finally` — so read the end state by WAITING for it, bounded, and print how long it took. A single read taken at the first moment is a coin toss that lands as a false red in a push-blocking suite. **⑳d "WE COULD NOT TELL" IS NOT "NOTHING CHANGED".** An empty result from a command whose exit status was never checked is not evidence; a cheap approximation (the tip commit) is not the question (the range being published). Both directions of that mistake skipped the gate entirely, which is the one outcome a gate must never reach by accident.

**ROUND 5 — A DOC THE GATE READS IS CODE, AND THE FAST *RUN* WAS STILL ABOUT WHATEVER WAS CHECKED OUT (2026-09-07, two defects from an adversarial read of round 4, both reproduced end to end with the real tracked hook and the REAL suites in throwaway repositories before they were fixed).**

**⑪ THE "NOT CODE" SET WAS A STATEMENT ABOUT HOW A PATH *LOOKS* (medium).** The docs-only classifier was the hand-written pattern `docs/*|*.md`, and several paths that look like documentation are **GATE INPUTS** — a suite in the tier table reads them and asserts on them, or the product serves them at runtime — so a "docs-only" push skipped BOTH tiers (the fast run and, because the docs-only exit sits above it, the heavy LAUNCH) and could ship a tree the gate would have refused. Measured, each reproduced in a scratch worktree at this branch's tip: `scripts/test-codex-effort-meta.mjs` (FAST) source-pins `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/kb-file-structure.md`, `docs/kb-features.md`, `docs/kb-bugfix-invariants.md` and `CHANGELOG.md` — renumbering the version marker in **only** `docs/kb-file-structure.md` gave `FAILED (2 of 108)`, and **this branch's own tip commit is exactly that push shape**; `test-plugin-loader` / `-trust` / `-security` (FAST) `cpSync` + parse `docs/examples/hello-plugin`, and an unparseable version there gave `16 FAILED (32 passed)` and made `test-plugin-trust` THROW; `docs/agent/*-manual.md` is RUNTIME PRODUCT DATA — `src/agent-routes.js` serves it to every agent CLI (`GET /api/agent/docs/:topic`, `AGENT_DOC_TOPICS`) out of the running checkout — and deleting `docs/agent/msg-manual.md` gave `1 FAILED (40 passed)`. The fix is a named `is_code_path()` in the hook whose first arms list the gate inputs — **and that list is NOT trusted**: `test-ci-gate` §4 DERIVES the set by scanning every gated suite's source (plus the scripts `npm run build` chains, because the fast tier is *build + suites*; they read no documentation today, which is a fact that can change with one commit) for whole-string `docs/…` / `*.md` literals that exist in the repo, adds `AGENT_DOC_TOPICS` parsed out of `src/agent-routes.js`, and then runs the hook's OWN `is_code_path` — extracted verbatim from the tracked file, never re-spelled — over all 21 of them, going red and NAMING any path the shipped hook still calls documentation. The anchoring is deliberate: a literal that merely appears inside a sentence or as a fixture VALUE (`'/w/README.md'`, `'please read README.md and fix the typo'` in test-image-cards / test-opencode-serve) is not a path this repo reads, and dragging the root `README.md` into the code set would empty the escape hatch — so the controls also assert that ordinary documentation (README.md, docs/getting-started.md, docs/terminal.md, docs/screenshots/**) still skips, with the **pre-round-5 pattern as the negative control** (it calls all 21 of them documentation, which is the defect) and this suite itself excluded from the scan by a MEASUREMENT rather than an assumption (its own controls hand doc paths to the classifier; the assert right there says test-ci-gate reads no documentation, so the day it does, it says so). End-to-end legs push a kb-only, an agent-manual-only and a hello-plugin-only commit through the REAL hook and require the fast tier to RUN, plus a README-only push that still skips.

**⑫ THE FAST TIER RAN AGAINST THE WORKING TREE (low) — invariant ⑭ in the last place it had not reached.** Round 2 fixed the heavy VERDICT (`--check-heavy --head=<sha>`) and round 4 fixed the green-marker SHORTCUT, but the fast RUN itself was a bare `node scripts/ci.mjs` in whatever tree the developer had checked out, with no knowledge of `PUSHED_SHAS`. Reproduced through the real hook: standing on `main`, pushing `refs/heads/feature` whose tip adds `src/broken.js` ⇒ the tier ran in a tree that did not contain that file, printed **ALL GREEN**, and let the ungated commit through; §4 asserted only that a fast run HAPPENED, never its SUBJECT. **We run it AT the sha rather than refusing the shape**, deliberately: refusing is the other honest answer and it is cheaper, but pushing a branch you are not standing on works today and the only bypass we ship is `VIBESPACE_SKIP_CI=1`, which skips the heavy verdict too — turning a working push into "use the total bypass" is exactly the *a gate people route around is not a gate* failure the split exists to remove. The ordinary push (every pushed sha IS HEAD) still runs in place and costs what it costs today, so the ≤2 min budget is untouched; only the rare mismatch pays for one `worktree add` (~3 s) and then the same tier. `fastGate({sha, isolate})` shares ONE `addScratchWorktree()` with heavyGate (same `vs-ci-<tier>-<sha8>-<pid>` naming, so the mutation harness's reaper recognises both), installs the same `OUTSIDE_SIGNALS` cleanup handlers, **writes NO `.git/ci-green`** (the marker's contract is "HEAD, clean, passed" — an isolated run at another commit proves nothing about the tree the next push would skip the tier for, and it SAYS so instead of going quiet), and the closing line NAMES its subject either way: `ALL GREEN … for <sha8> (isolated worktree at the commit being pushed)` vs `… (this working tree)`. Distinct shas only, so a multi-ref push of one commit runs once. `test-ci-gate` now asserts the SUBJECT of the fast call (`--isolate --sha=<the pushed tip>`) and `test-ci-heavy-launch` (3) drives the REAL `fastGate` on a stub repository — a probe suite reports which TREE it ran in — with the in-place run as the control and the one isolating line removed as the negative control. Known boundary, inherited from the heavy tier: the tier TABLE is the running gate's, while the SUITE SOURCES are the pushed commit's.

**MEASURED (round 5).** `test-ci-gate` 136 (was 114), `test-ci-heavy-launch` 81 (was 73), census 186 = 73 + 97 + 16 inside `npm run build`, mutation battery 23 (three new — the hook's fast-run subject, ci.mjs's `--isolate` on the fast tier, and the gate-input arms of `is_code_path` — each RED naming the asserts that die with it, `--only=round 5` in 32 s). FAST tier: build 1.8 s + 72 suites green in 106.8 s; the 73rd, `test-chat-e2e`, was RED for a vendor `api_error` on the CI subscription and reproduces identically on the untouched base commit, so it is a fact about this box's credential, not about the change (`test-discovery-interpret`'s docker-overlay `lsof` stderr leg is red on this branch's base too and is already fixed on master by bc74f2ae). The whole hook story walked end to end against the REAL tracked hook: a kb-only push RUNS the fast tier · an agent-manual-only push RUNS it · a hello-plugin-only push RUNS it · a README-only push still skips · a ref whose tip is not HEAD is gated `--isolate --sha=<tip>` and says so · the ordinary push still runs in place · two refs at one commit run it once.

**INVARIANTS ADDED (⑳f-⑳g).** **⑳f A `.md` PATH THE GATE READS IS A CODE PATH.** "Documentation" is not a spelling — it is "nothing the gate reads and nothing the product serves". A hand-written "this is not code" set is a claim about a set that changes every time a suite adds a `read()`, so DERIVE it from the suites' own sources and make the check NAME the file it found; measure, never assert. **⑳g A RULE CORRECTED IN ONE PLACE IS OWED TO EVERY CONSUMER OF THAT FACT — INCLUDING THE ONE THAT DOES THE WORK.** ⑭ was fixed for the heavy verdict (round 2) and for the marker shortcut (round 4) while the fast tier's actual RUN kept gating whatever tree happened to be checked out, because the test asked "did a run happen" and never "about what". An assert that a step OCCURRED is not an assert about its SUBJECT.

**ROUND 6 — WHAT A RUN IS A VERDICT *ABOUT* WHEN THE TABLE AND THE SOURCES COME FROM DIFFERENT COMMITS, AND HOW MUCH OF THE BUDGET ONE PUSH MAY SPEND (2026-09-07, two defects from an adversarial read of round 5, both reproduced against the real ci.mjs / the real tracked hook before they were fixed).**

**⑬ A SUITE THE PUSHED COMMIT DOES NOT CONTAIN WAS A RED, SO EVERY OLDER REF WAS UNPUSHABLE (high).** Round 5's own closing note — "the tier TABLE is the running gate's, the SUITE SOURCES are the pushed commit's" — was written as a boundary and is in fact a **defect**: `runSuite` spawns `node <root>/scripts/<name>.mjs` with no existence check, so a name this gate's table has and the gated commit does not exits `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` ⇒ RED, and the fast tier is fail-fast, so the push is hard-blocked. Reproduced with the REAL module against REAL history: `node scripts/ci.mjs --isolate --sha=5d54ffe5` (master's tip) ran 51 green suites and then died on `Cannot find module /tmp/vs-ci-fast-5d54ffe5-861442/scripts/test-ci-gate.mjs` — because master is missing exactly the two fast suites this branch adds. **Once this gate is integrated that is every branch and tag that predates it**: measured across this repository, master's tip is missing 2 of 73 fast suites, `master~300` 42 of 73, and the `v2.30.0` tag all 73 (the same shape reaches the heavy tier, which is isolated on EVERY run — 10 of 97 at `master~300`). The push shapes that hit it are ordinary: `git push --tags` (41 here), `git push --all` (315 branches), or re-pushing any older branch from a checkout standing elsewhere. The fix is the smaller of the two the verifier offered — **an absence, not a verdict**: `runSuite(s, {absentIsSkip, sha})` skips a file that does not exist at the gated commit, LOUDLY (`⊘ <name> — SKIPPED: not present at <sha8>`), both tiers count them, the fast tier’s closing line carries `— N of M suites ran; K not present at that commit` plus a line naming them, and the heavy MARKER records `absent: [...]` so `suites: 97` is never a number the record itself contradicts. It is scoped to isolated runs ON PURPOSE: in place, the table and the tree come from one checkout, so a missing file means this tree disagrees with its own table — a RED, and one `--census` already reports as a ghost inside `npm run build`. Two vacuity guards come with it, because "skip the missing ones" and "claim a green for a run of zero suites" are one edit apart: a fast run in which EVERY suite was absent prints `NO VERDICT — the fast tier could not gate <sha>` and exits **0** (an absence is not evidence of breakage; blocking every old ref is the defect being fixed), and a heavy run in which every suite was absent writes NO marker and says so — the same vacuous green `--only` already refuses on a typo. Measured end to end after the fix: master's tip ⇒ ALL GREEN, 71 of 73, the two absent named, exit 0; the `v2.30.0` tag ⇒ 73 of 73 absent, `NO VERDICT`, exit 0 in 0.8 s (its `npm run build` still ran, and passed, in 452 ms — the build is deliberately still a RED if it fails at the gated commit).

**⑭ ONE PUSH, N BILLED CHAT TURNS (medium).** Round 5 turned the fast run into a LOOP over the distinct pushed shas, so the whole ≤2 min budget — and the real haiku turn inside it (`test-chat-e2e`, real quota) — was multiplied by the number of refs, **inside the live SSH session**, which is the timeout the split exists to fit under. Reproduced with the real hook in a throwaway repo: a three-ref push ⇒ THREE fast runs (in place for HEAD, isolated for the other two). The hook now picks **exactly one fast subject per push**: HEAD when HEAD is among the pushed shas (the ordinary push, in place, byte-for-byte what it did before), otherwise the NEWEST of them by committer date (`git rev-list --no-walk=sorted`, accepted only if the answer is one of the shas actually being pushed — an annotated tag peels to a commit nobody named, and the first pushed ref is the fallback). The others are **not ungated**: `--heavy-launch` still runs for every pushed sha, and that tier is where a multi-ref push gets its per-commit coverage — so the hook SAYS which commits the fast tier did not look at, because a silent one-of-three reads as "all of them were gated". `fast_subjects="$subject"` is the guard, and setting it back to `"$distinct"` is the round-5 hook verbatim, which is the negative control.

**MEASURED (round 6).** `test-ci-gate` 153 (was 136), `test-ci-heavy-launch` 93 (was 81, 28.3 s — the price of driving the REAL `fastGate` five more times plus two real heavy runs), census 186 = 73 + 97 + 16 inside `npm run build` (1.8 s), mutation battery 27 (four new — the existence check, both vacuity guards and the hook's one-subject selection — each RED naming the asserts that die with it, `--only=round 6` in ~3 min). End to end against the REAL tracked hook driving the REAL `fastGate` (only `--check-heavy` / `--heavy-launch` stubbed, because a real heavy launch would take this box's machine lock for sixteen minutes): a lightweight old tag, an annotated old tag (the pushed sha is the TAG OBJECT) and an old branch all run ONE fast tier, name their skipped suites and exit 0 · a three-ref push runs the fast tier ONCE, launches three heavy runs and names the two commits it did not gate.

**INVARIANTS ADDED (⑳h-⑳i).** **⑳h A NAME THE GATED COMMIT DOES NOT CONTAIN IS AN ABSENCE, NOT A FAILURE.** When the TABLE and the SOURCES come from two different commits — which is every isolated run, i.e. the whole heavy tier and any non-HEAD push — a missing suite is nothing to judge; say so, count it, and put the count in the sentence that reports the result, because "ALL GREEN (97 suites)" for a run of 55 is a claim the record itself contradicts. The corollary is the vacuity guard: the moment "missing = skip" exists, "everything missing = green" is one step away, and a run that judged nothing must claim nothing (⑪) *without* blocking a push it has no evidence against. **⑳i A GATE'S COST IS PER PUSH, NOT PER REF.** A loop over the pushed refs multiplies a budget that was measured once — and here it also multiplies real spend and the SSH idle timeout the tier is sized for. One subject per push, chosen by a stated rule, with the refs it did not cover NAMED; per-ref coverage belongs to the tier that already runs per sha in the background.

**INVARIANTS.** ① A suite is in exactly one tier or in EXCLUDED with a reason — no third state, and `npm run build` says so. ② A heavy row without a `why` is a census failure. ③ The marker names a commit, so the run must have BEEN that commit (isolate) or the tree must have been clean (in place). ④ Anything launched from a git hook gets `gitEnvFrom(process.env)`. ⑤ Both tiers run in the Actions mirror, as two PARALLEL jobs (heavy is not a consequence of fast; `needs: fast` would only delay the slow signal). ⑥ Moving a suite between tiers is a measurement, not an opinion — put the number in the `why`. ⑦ A `--only=` run writes a marker but never a CLEARING one: a partial green is not evidence the tier passed (a partial RED still blocks — a suite really did fail there). ⑧ A check that runs inside `npm run build` may only read what a build reads — several browser suites build a PARTIAL COPY of the tree in a throwaway worktree, so a build-time assert comparing files outside the copied set fails there for reasons unrelated to the code under test (measured: the package.json wiring pin turned test-window-menu into a 300 s timeout, which then read as "test-window-menu is red on master" — it wasn't; the wiring pins moved into test-ci-gate). ⑨ Retry-once never becomes retry-twice, and a retried pass is always NAMED. ⑩ **ONE heavy tier per MACHINE** — the lock lives at literal `/tmp`, not in the checkout and not at `os.tmpdir()` (that one follows TMPDIR, i.e. it names a process environment, not a machine), because the resources the suites claim are machine-wide; a new "run the tier" entry point takes it too. ⑪ **A run that did not happen claims nothing** — no green, no red, a `skipped` note, exit 3, and every surface says "no verdict" rather than staying silent. ⑫ **Refuse at t=0, not at t=16 min**: any decision that determines whether a run can produce a verdict is made and announced BEFORE the work, and the closing line never claims a verdict nobody recorded. ⑬ **Advice in a block message must be reachable** — never point at a door that only opens from the other side. ⑭ **The verdict is about the refs being PUSHED**, never about whichever branch happens to be checked out — the heavy verdict (round 2), the green-marker shortcut (round 4) AND the fast RUN itself (round 5: `--isolate --sha=<tip>` in a scratch worktree when a pushed ref's tip is not HEAD, and a closing line that names its subject) — but the COST is per push, not per ref (round 6, ⑳i): exactly one fast subject per push (HEAD if it is being pushed, else the newest pushed sha), with the commits it did not cover NAMED and left to the heavy tier, which already launches per sha. ⑮ **No FAST-tier suite claims a machine-global name** (a literal port it binds, a fixed `/tmp` path it creates or removes) — transitively, including any slice it launches; `machineGlobalFixtures` asserts it, with the pre-fix shapes as negative controls in `scripts/fixtures/machine-global-shapes/`. ⑯ **A killed run cleans up after itself** — supersession means SIGTERM is a normal exit path, and node's default SIGTERM does not run `finally`. ⑰ **A kill path needs positive identity; a read path does not** — `pidStillRunning` trusts a record that names nothing, `looksLikeHeavyRun` (the supersede gate) asks `/proc` and answers NO when it cannot tell. ⑱ **An interrupted run never stamps a verdict, and a SIGNAL HANDLER IS NOT AN ABORT in a synchronous runner** — heavyGate asks `abandoned()` synchronously between suites (pid file gone / lock taken / a child killed by a signal somebody SENT us — `OUTSIDE_SIGNALS` = SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP, never a crash signal: see ⑳a), because a handler cannot preempt `spawnSync` and the failure it would otherwise record is one WE caused; and it exits **4**, never 0 (⑳b). ⑲ **A cleanup assert must outlive the tool that cleans up for you** — killing during `git worktree add` measures git's own rollback, not ours; wait until the operation whose cleanup you are testing has completed. ⑳ **A suite that dirties the REPOSITORY shrinks the window rather than trusting cleanup** — `finally`, `process.on('exit')` and signal handlers all fail the same way (a killed process, or one sitting in `spawnSync`), and this class was measured twice in one afternoon: the mutation harness left the pre-push hook mutated, and test-ci-gate stranded its dirty-tree probe, which costs the next push its green marker. test-ci-gate's probe now exists only until the run under test has CAPTURED the dirty tree (it says so on its own stdout, ~200 ms), plus a self-heal at start, plus the handlers. And an ABORTED run says ABORTED — "HEAVY TIER GREEN" beside "NO VERDICT WRITTEN" is still a sentence somebody can quote. ㉒ **Retry-once is for a flaky FIXTURE, never for a failure we caused** — before re-running a failed suite, ask whether this run has been abandoned (a superseded run's suite dies of our own group SIGTERM), because the retry costs a full suite budget, holds the MACHINE LOCK while it runs, and its answer is discarded anyway. ㉑ **A marker KIND has three readers** — `ci.mjs` writes it, `GET /api/ci-heavy` serves it and the Diagnostics report renders it; a kind that reaches only the CLI is a verdict the UI silently DROPS, and its absence reads exactly like "nobody has pushed lately" (⑪ in reverse). test-ci-gate §6 derives the API leg from ci.mjs's own kind list, so a fifth kind has to be served too, and pins the renderer on `skipped` by name — `pid` is not a verdict there (an in-flight run is the RUNNING row), so "render every kind" would be the wrong rule. Round 6 adds the same rule for a marker FIELD that changes what another field MEANS: `absent` (the suites the gated commit did not contain) travels ci.mjs → `ci:status` → `/api/ci-heavy` → the Diagnostics report — FOUR readers, because a green row printing "97 suites" for a run of 55 is the marker-kind lesson one field smaller. The two greps have their pre-fix mutations as controls; the CLI leg is FUNCTIONAL (a real marker through the real `--status`, with an absent-less marker as the control) because that is the reader an operator actually runs.

**LANES, AN ABANDONED SHA, THE IMPACT-SCOPED TIER, AND THE 414-SECOND SUITE (2026-09-15, owner: "heavy gate太占用时间了吧 不能优化一下").** MEASURED on `data/ci-heavy/d0e7a8d4.{log,green}`: **4472 s wall = 40 min WAITING on the machine lock** behind a run for d5e3e587 — a sha that had been AMENDED AWAY, an ancestor of nothing, unpushable, so the round-2 rule queued behind its full 40-min budget — **plus 34.5 min (2069 s) of 108 suites run STRICTLY SEQUENTIALLY** on a 32-cpu box (writer-sweep 414 s, opencode-s9 226, desktop-resume-paging 225, desktop-app-keeper 104, queue-steer 87, restore-liveness 86, client-boot 72, jobs-engine 71).
